utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Dzemail Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a witness whose statement we intend to tender under provisions of 92 bis. I'd ask if we could have an exhibit number assigned for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 442 contains Mr. Becirevic's account of the events in Bratunac municipality prior to and during the takeover of Bratunac in April of 1991. At that time, he was the chief of the National Secretariat for Defence of the municipality. He describes the removal of weapons from the stores of the Territorial Defence. He gives a brief account of the development of and interaction between the SDS party and the SDA party and Miroslav Deronjic's significant role in the political and military developments in the Bratunac area. The statement goes on to describe the events surrounding the mobilisation or call-up during the war in Croatia and the build-up of the JNA resources in the area of Bratunac upon their withdrawal from Croatia. He describes the founding of their respective Crisis Staffs in 1991. Mr. Becirevic's statement goes on to describe the wounding and killing of several Muslims in an ambush in the area of Kravica. It goes on to describe the establishment by Mr. Deronjic of a separate police force and the provision of military training for Serbs by the JNA. Prosecution Exhibit 442 continues with the actual takeover of the municipality in mid-April of 1992 and describes the appearance of Arkan's Tigers. In the statement, Mr. Becirevic goes on to describe seeing Mr. Deronjic in a camouflage uniform riding in a JNA armoured personnel carrier in the area of Konjevic Polje. The statement describes the fierce battle that ensued in this area. The statement continues with the description of a counter-offensive launched from Serbia in the Bratunac area in January of 1993 after the Muslim forces took the area of Cerska. It describes troops coming from Ljubovija and Bajina Basta in Serbia, an offensive that lasted until the 15th of March, 1993. We will seek at this stage to ask Mr. Becirevic some additional matters not contained in his statement, as well as I seek his comment on a number of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, my first question to you is: When were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I served in the Yugoslav People's Army from 1980 to 1981. And as for my involvement in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I served from end April 1992 to 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, when I managed to get out of Srebrenica and go to Tuzla. That's when I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was your profession after you were demobilised, immediately after?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after my demobilisation, I continued for a couple of months to work in the military court in Tuzla as an investigative judge up until the end of the state of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the military court was abolished, whereupon I continued to work in a civilian court, the higher court of Tuzla, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I am a lawyer, and I currently have my own private law practice in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 4 of your statement, which is now Prosecution Exhibit 442, you describe the removal of weapons from the Territorial Defence building in Bratunac. My question to you in supplement to your statement is: Did you personally witness any of the removal of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw with my own eyes when the Yugoslav People's Army arrived in 1989. At the time, I was working for an enterprise called Duhan, a tobacco factory in Bratunac, and the factory was located directly opposite military depots. The depots held all the weaponry of the Territorial Defence of Bratunac, and the entire population of Bratunac contributed to the purchase of those weapons. In 1989, as I said, the Yugoslav People's Army arrived with about a dozen military vehicles and trucks, and all these arms were taken out and transported to Ljubovija in Serbia. I know nothing further about the fate of those arms. So the distance between the enterprise where I was working from the depots was barely 50 metres, and more importantly, from my office I could see what was going on, and I even went outside to look. Nobody offered any resistance when these weapons were being removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I might draw your attention now to paragraph 5 of your statement. You describe yourself as one of the first to organise and join the SDA party in Bratunac. Could I ask you to simply list the other significant members of the SDA party in Bratunac in -- at the time of its founding.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It was Nezid Muratovic, Dzevad Gusic, Dubicic Nijaz, Semsudin Durakovic, Abid Sirucic, and myself who set up the SDA, or rather, made a motion, an initiative for its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again, your statement deals in detail with the founding and membership of the SDS party. What I would ask you to deal with now is: Are you familiar with a part of that party or a committee on that party called the Initiative Board? And if so, I would ask you to list the names of the members of that board.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That body was called the Initiative Council or the Initiative Board of the Party of Democratic Action, and I just enumerated the people who were on that board. I can also mention Hasan Smailovic as a member, Safet Dzanic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: -- and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I'm actually asking now about the other party, the SDS party, not the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: As for the SDS, the first founding members were Miroslav Deronjic, Jovan Nikolic, Nedjo Nikolic, Zoran Tesic, Zoran Radic, and some other Serbs whom I mentioned in my statement as having established the SDS party in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, what -- can you describe for us, during the period relevant to your testimony, can you describe what positions he held in the SDS party in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Miroslav Deronjic, apart from being the president of the SDS in Bratunac, also occupied the position of president of the SDS Crisis Staff of Bratunac. He was also president of the war commissioner's office for Bratunac and discharged a number of other functions. He was a member of a commission whose exclusive task - and this was a three-member commission - was to dispose of and allocate funds from the SDS account.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to comment on what knowledge you have regarding the relationship between the SDS board in Bratunac and the SDS leadership in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The SDS party in Bratunac received orders directly from the SDS in Sarajevo, and I remember very clearly that whenever we from the SDA tried to agree with the Bratunac SDS on some sort of division of authority after the first democratic election, and whenever we would manage to reach an agreement, the SDS would ask for a timeout of one or two days for somebody to go to Sarajevo, to talk to Radovan Karadzic, the president of the SDS for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So they got instructions from Radovan Karadzic. But whenever we would resume talks to agree on the further division of authority, they would ignore us and renege on the agreement that we had reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us the names of some of the members of the Bratunac SDS that actually travelled to Sarajevo in the manner you've described?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, it was Miroslav Deronjic, Radoljub Djukanovic, president of the executive board of the Bratunac Municipal Assembly, where I was a member too; then there was also Zoran Tesic and Jovan Nikolic. So these are the people who often went to Sarajevo to the head office of the SDS for consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has a binder of ten exhibits it would seek to use with this witness. Could I ask that an exhibit number be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 443.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you take a look at a document. It is Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 2. My question to you is: Have you had a chance to review this prior to your testimony this morning, and do you recognise any of the names that are listed on this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not have occasion to see this document before starting my testimony. As for the names listed here, I know all these people personally. The signatory of this document is the president of the executive board of the SDS for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Rajko Dukic, general manager of the bauxite mine in Milici. It belonged to Konjevic Polje municipality previously and then became a separate municipality. In 1991, which is the date of this document, these people were authorised to allocate SDS funds. I see the first name on the list, Milenko Katanic. He is a clerk in the municipal administration of Bratunac. I knew him personally because I also worked in the municipal administration. There was also Miroslav Deronjic, president of the SDS and president of the Crisis Staff, and Zoran Radic, also a member of the Crisis Staff and of the SDS executive board for Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, your statement is quite a detailed one, and there is a matter of which you have an awful lot of personal knowledge, that is, the -- the Muslim community's reaction to a mobilisation order. It's dealt with in great detail in your statement and it's also been the subject of testimony by other witnesses, so I will not go into it at this point. But I would ask you one question regarding it, and the particular aspect of it I would like to ask you about here is there came a time when there was an attempt to remove a list of reservists that was in your custody; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is: What knowledge do you have with respect to were other municipalities -- were similar attempts made to obtain possession of that -- a similar list from other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do know that in other municipalities as well there were attempts to take away these military files by force, in municipalities where Bosniaks were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention now to the area of Kravica and specifically to a number -- or to an event that occurred there. Do you know the event that I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor probably means the events that had to do with the killing in Kravica on the 3rd of September, 1991, when there was an ambush in the evening. Four Bosniaks were attacked for no reason whatsoever, and they were moving along the road from Konjevic Polje towards Glogova -- rather, Bratunac. At a curve, from a rock in the village of Kajici near Kravica, they were ambushed. In that ambush, two young men were killed and two were seriously wounded. The murderers who had committed the killing are from Kravica; Radinko Milanovic, nicknamed Mali Raso, and the other one is Marko Markovic from Cerska, municipality of Ljubovija, Serbia. So they are the direct perpetrators of the crime, upon instructions of the SDS from Bratunac in order to cause tensions between the Bosniaks and the Serbs in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, what was the consequence of this event?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after this killing, the Bosniak people was frightened. There was an escalation of tensions in the municipality of Bratunac. The following day, the road was closed temporarily. People came from Sarajevo - they had to come from Sarajevo, from the Presidency, from the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, top people - in order to try to ease the tensions, because there was a danger of having a war break out then in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. From the Presidency, Ganic came, as well as Nikola Koljevic. They came by helicopter to Bratunac to try to calm down the situation in the municipality. It was agreed that these two delegations go to Kravica together and that they try to establish how this killing occurred. Finally, Koljevic went on his own to Kravica without allowing a proper investigation and without making it possible for the perpetrators to be found immediately; that is to say, they forbade the legal authorities of the MUP from Bratunac to come and investigate who committed the crime and who organised the murder. After that, there were replacements, or rather, a resignation of the head of the MUP and the commander of the police were forced. Nezid Muratovic was in this position then as head of MUP, and Nikola Mandic was commander of the police force. After them --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was one of the consequences, as you describe in your statement, that Serbs left the area and also the appearance of artillery on the Serb side of the border in Ljubovija?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after that, that was one of the consequences too, that the moving out of Serbs to Ljubovija was staged. Allegedly after this killing that they had committed, there was some kind of danger looming over the Serbs in Bratunac. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At that time were patrols initiated by both the Muslim community and the Serb community as tensions rose?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was agreed with the top echelons of the B & H MUP to reinforce the reserve MUP force by Serbs and Bosniaks so that these tensions would be eased. However, every village, Bosniak and Serb, at the time had to have guards in the evening because there was fear from having some groups, paramilitary groups, coming in from Serbia and attacking people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time period, did you become aware of arms being distributed to the Serb community, members of the Serb community?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I learned that, after these events, weapons were being distributed and that also what started was the mass proliferation of weapons from Serbia. In the region of Voljavica, in the village of Pobrdje, an attempt was made to get weapons from Ljubovija there by boats. This was prevented at a given point in time, but it nevertheless continued later, that is to say, the supply of weapons. And one of the Serbs who took part in the supply of weapons was arrested, handed over to the MUP in Bratunac, but the next day he was released, which is to say that the MUP -- or rather, individual employees of the MUP took part in this arming of Serbs in Bratunac from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what, if any, arms were possessed by the Muslim community and any attempts to distribute them.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Muslim community at that time did not have any weapons whatsoever. As I've already said, the arms of the TO were taken by the JNA. And as for privately owned weapons, there were some hunting guns that some Bosniaks had. At that time, an attempt was made to obtain weapons. Serbs themselves were selling trophy weapons at high prices, those that they had been issued themselves, the so-called Dobosari, the PAP rifles, and they were selling them at a high price to Bosniaks. But this was only done by people who wanted to earn a profit in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to now take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 3. It's a book of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would note for the Chamber that I will simply be seeking to mark this for identification and complete its foundation with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this document, it's a lengthy document, purporting to be a book of minutes of meetings held in Bratunac. Have you had, in the last few days, an opportunity to read this book of minutes thoroughly?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: This is a book of minutes on the establishment of the illegal Assembly of Bratunac, that is to say, of the Serb Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read the events -- read the book of minutes and the events described in it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not have an opportunity of seeing this minutes earlier, but I do know that a Serb Municipality of the Municipality of Bratunac was established in December 1991. The government -- or rather, the executive committee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Becirevic, just concentrate on what counsel is asking you and just limit your questions -- your answers, if you would, to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Earlier this week, did you have an opportunity to read what you have before you now?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of the events described in that book of minutes of which you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. personal knowledge, are they accurately reflected?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are fully well-described here, because I knew, Your Honours, that the SDS had established a Serb Assembly of Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: -- as well as a government --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I want to now draw your attention -- in your statement you talk about JNA military presence in Ljubovija. My question to you is: Were you able to see the military resources assembled in Ljubovija? And if so, could you please describe with as much detail as possible what those resources were.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I personally saw artillery being positioned on the other side of the Drina, in the region of Ljubovija, namely, in the region of Krs. These were tanks, Howitzers, and other heavy artillery pieces whose barrels were aimed at the municipality of Bratunac in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was common knowledge among all the citizens of the municipality of Bratunac. Everybody could see this with their very own eyes, and so could I, since I worked --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please approximate for us the number of tanks that you saw and the number of Howitzers that you saw.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at Krs itself, which is 2 kilometres away from Bratunac on the other side of the Drina, only at one place there were at least two heavy weapons, a tank and an APC, with their barrels pointing at settlements in the Bratunac municipality. At another point, facing Voljavica and Bjelavica, there were a few artillery pieces whose barrels were pointing at Bratunac and the settlements around Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to March of 1992. During that period of time, did you become aware that members of the Serb community were being secretly trained in military matters by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I knew that full well because I had that type of a job. Citizens who were Bosniaks came to see me every day, and they expressed their dissatisfaction over the fact that training was taking place in the village of Vranesevici, training of Serb forces by officers of the Yugoslav People's Army. After such pressures exerted upon the leadership of the Bratunac municipality by the citizens - and I was part of the leadership - I and the president of the municipality of Bratunac, the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac, personally went to the corps command of the Yugoslav People's Army in Tuzla and we asked the commander, Jankovic, and his assistant to tell us what kind of unit this was and also what the possibilities were for having it removed from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you went to the headquarters of the Tuzla Corps, who specifically did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Specifically we talked to Jankovic. We were received by Jankovic and his assistant Gavric, who I personally knew from earlier on, because he came to see me at the secretariat when he came to mobilise wartime units that he needed in 1991 for the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did they tell you in response to your complaint about the secret training by the officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: They said to us, quite literally, Your Honours, that right then they didn't know what kind of unit this was and that they, within two days, would send two officers, Sadic and Simic, to come to Bratunac and to go to the actual site with us so that we would inspect this locality and see what kind of unit this was. Two days later, when they were supposed to come to Bratunac, they simply didn't show up. We telephoned them. The president spoke personally, and I was right next to him in his office because I was greatly interested in this. Gavric answered the telephone and he said that they had established that this was not any unit from the area of responsibility of the Tuzla Corps or was it a unit from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the JNA. Rather, this was a unit that had come from Yugoslavia, and they had no authority whatsoever over that unit and they could not help us on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the area where this training was being conducted, was it under the area of responsibility of the Tuzla Corps?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was in the area of responsibility of the Tuzla Corps, but before the war there had never been any JNA unit stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to ask that you take a look at a series of two documents that were generated in the third week of April 1992. The first one is Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 4. I'm going to ask that you read two sentences, first a sentence under number 1 and then the sentence under number 3, and then comment on that.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order on the establishment of Territorial Defence staffs that was signed by the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Bratunac. Article 1: "Defence tasks in the territory of the Serbian Municipality of Bratunac shall be taken over by the Territorial Defence of the Serb Municipality of Bratunac." 3: "All decisions related to the use of the Territorial Defence shall be made by the Crisis Staff upon suggestions made by the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence." My comment would be as follows, Your Honours: At that time, I was in the municipality of Bratunac. I worked there. I worked there until the 17th of April, 1992, and I did not have an opportunity of familiarising myself with this document; that is to say, that all of this was done secretly at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- based upon your observations and experience from that time period, is there a connection between what's contained in this document and the training of people by the JNA that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it can be seen indeed that there is a link between the training that was being carried out in Vranesevici and this order that was issued by the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you now to take a look at a document from the 16th of April, 1992. It's tab 5 of Prosecution Exhibit 443. I'd ask you to take a look at this document. I'd ask you: Do you recognise the seal on the document? And then finally, if you would summarise its contents for us.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not have the opportunity of seeing this document before either, but I can state here that I am familiar with the stamp affixed by the Serb Municipality of Bratunac, this Serb Municipality being established in December 1991 although there was a legal Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. This means that by this order everything had been prepared in order to occupy Bratunac, and the actual occupation took place a day later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that this document deals with the mobilisation of members of the Serb community to create a defence force?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The first item here shows that a decision was passed on the general mobilisation of the Serb people. And this was done on the basis of a decision of the Presidency of the Serb people of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the staff or the Serb Municipality proclaimed general mobilisation on that day for all citizens who were ethnic Serbs and who were of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you just referred to a takeover, I believe, on the next day. So I would draw your attention now to the 17th of April. Can you describe -- did there come a time during the course of that day that you saw men you believed to be members of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 17th of April, 1992 I went to work and I arrived in the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac, that is to say, that I had intended to work on that day, to continue working. As I was passing by Fontana in Bratunac, I noticed some people who I did not know and who were armed. However, before that, on TV, I saw the occupation of Bijeljina on the 31st of March, 1992 and Zvornik on the 8th of April, 1992, so I noticed paramilitary formations that had come from Serbia. These were Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and members of the Yugoslav army. That is to say, that there were three types of uniforms and men wearing these uniforms were guarding the entrance to the Fontana Hotel. I asked around and I established that a meeting was being held there regarding the surrender of the municipality of Bratunac, and the legal organs of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina were also supposed to hand over the municipality of Bratunac to these paramilitaries who had come from Serbia. They had different insignia. I noticed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just wait a minute. We have read your statement, Mr. Becirevic, and counsel are just asking you some additional questions, So just wait until he asks you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you: Of the paramilitary units that you are describing as being from Serbia, can you simply just list the ones that you were able to recognise.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Your Honours, I recognised Arkan's men, Seselj's men, and there were some people who were wearing the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The three groups that you have mentioned, were they intermingled among each other or did they seem to be separate in their location and in their interaction?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, they were intermingled. Their objective was to guard the people who were attending the negotiations, the meeting, at the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around this time period, were you shown a copy of a proclamation of -- relating to what was going on in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had the opportunity of receiving a copy of this proclamation issued by the Yugoslav People's Army. The proclamation said that the legal authorities are being respected and that all faiths are being respected. An ironical sentence was added, that one loves one's brother no matter what faith that brother has. What was also asked for was the surrender of weapons, the surrender of weapons by Bosniak paramilitaries, the way they called them, Bosniak paramilitary forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: -- the signature said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I'd like to now ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 6. This document concerns the disarming of citizens. My question to you is: Do you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this signature is one I cannot recognise. However, I know that such a decision was passed on the disarming of citizens who possess weapons, citizens of the municipality of Bratunac. This was issued by the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And around this time period, were there activities by the forces -- the Serb forces in town consistent with disarming of -- the disarming of the Muslim community? Simply yes or no, if possible.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask that the witness be shown tab 7 of Prosecution Exhibit 443.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this is another document related to Bratunac, issued on the 16th of June, 1992. I'd ask you to look down the names listed on this document, and if you would identify which names you are familiar with and which names you -- if there are any that you are not familiar with, please indicate.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are five names here. Of those, I know number 2, Miroslav Deronjic, number 3, Zoran Tesic - he was the secretary of the SDS - I know Jovan Nikolic, and Stanko Petrovic. So the four of them, I knew them all personally. I cooperated and worked with them. As for the first name, Dragan -- Dr. Dragan Djokanovic, I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this document concerns the establishment of a Municipal War Presidency. To your knowledge, was such a War Presidency established in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that a War Presidency was set up by the Serb Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you now to take a look at tab 8 of Prosecution Exhibit 443. It's a document dated the very next day, the 17th of June, 1992. Would you tell us who is the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the author of this document is the president of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. And he confirms the appointment of the members of the War Presidency for the Serbian Municipality of Bratunac by way of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, on the 17th of April, 1992, is it true that you left the town of Bratunac and went to Konjevic Polje, where you remained until the 15th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on that particular day, when I saw what was going on in Bratunac, that the units had turned up there, I barely managed to escape and went to my native Konjevic Polje area, where I stayed until the 15th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, your statement deals in some detail with the events of Glogova. My question to you is: After what happened in Glogova, was there an event in Konjevic Polje where members of Koljevic -- or people in the community of Konjevic Polje blocked JNA forces as they were attempting to leave Bosnia? If so, I'd ask you to briefly describe what occurred between the people of Konjevic Polje and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we received an order to the effect that the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, or Konjevic Polje-Drinjaca road be kept open up until the 19th of May, 1992 -- or rather, this period of time was pinpointed by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was extended for a three-day period. So we kept the road open, in fact, until the 22nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on the 22nd of May, 1992, did you and other members of your community block the road to passing JNA traffic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: We did not block the road on the 22nd because the JNA had already left Central Bosnia-Herzegovina and was moving towards Serbia. However, many units stayed behind. They just changed their insignia. They stayed behind on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a blockade was set up in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On what day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at one particular point -- or rather, on the 22nd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked -- just listen to what counsel ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On what date, sir?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The 29th was when the road was closed, the 29th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that, in the months following this, that there was substantial fighting and attacks in the area of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, that is right. There was substantial fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of this fighting, did you have opportunity to see aircraft involved in this fighting?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, planes belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army overflew the area on a daily basis and shelled the area with heavy bombs that were referred to as Krmace in Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and Kamenica, which made a separate enclave surrounded on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time period after the official withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army, were you aware of participation in these -- in these war activities by members of the now renamed Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I was aware of that. I knew that those units had just changed their uniforms, or rather, insignia, but that they had the weapons they did before to carry on the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to attack the territory of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this period of time, were there any other units that you could identify or wore some distinctive uniform that you could see?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: During the attack, Your Honours, of the area around Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and Kamenica, in addition to the Yugoslav People's Army units and the local Serb units, also taking part in the area were the so-called Red Berets, or rather, Arkan's and Seselj's men, and they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fighting to gain control of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to January of 1993. Was there a major offensive by Serb forces during that time period in the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Serb forces launched an all-out heavy offensive in the free areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica from the 13th of January onwards right up until the 17th of April, 1993, when the territory was occupied and the people forced to withdraw to the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to learn from where the forces that were -- you were opposing, where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was able to learn this, that the units in fact were coming from Serbia and that they had crossed the bridge at Zvornik, they had crossed the bridge, the Ljubovija bridge at Bratunac, they had also crossed the bridge at Bajina Basta, so that from three flanks, three corps arrived and, together with the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, they attacked the free territory of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During this time period, did you see aircraft involved? If so, would you describe the type of aircraft for us.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did see aircraft flying over the area from the direction of Serbia, and they were shooting and targeting the free territory at random, which was Konjevic Polje and Cerska at that time, and similarly they used helicopters who were flying at a very low altitude and, with guided missiles and bombs, they targeted the positions of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I want to now move on to March of 1993. Did there come a time when the Serb forces were successful and the members of the Muslim community in this pocket, as well as the soldiers defending them, withdrew to the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the civilians from Cerska Kamenica gathered together in Konjevic Polje, and all of them after that were forced to withdraw in the direction of Srebrenica, and that was on the 15th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many civilians were in this group?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, from Cerska and Kamenica, about 5.000 civilians came in. And from Konjevic Polje, at least 5.000 civilians had to withdraw as well, so that from these three enclaves, there were at least 10.000 civilians who were having to be on the move towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in this group, how many soldiers were -- were part of that group?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that group were the remnants of the BH army, the stragglers who were broken up by the enemy forces, and there were approximately 100 to 150 people holding this line for the civilians to ensure that they did not remain in the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to now ask you -- moving to a different subject, ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 10. It will be displayed on the television monitor in front of you. Do you recognise the site depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I do recognise this. These are the grounds of a religious site, the mosque, in fact, in Konjevic Polje, my native town. And the mosque itself in the course of 1993, more exactly on the 15th of March of that year, without any reason whatsoever was destroyed by tanks. It was attacked. And quite simply, it was attacked and targeted by tank shells and grenades. Two or three months later, when I went back to my native town, all I saw was a mass of rubble. That was all that was left of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It was in ruins. And what I can see here now on the photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- were you present when this mosque was fired upon?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was present -- actually, I was just a couple of hundred metres away when the tanks arrived, to within 50 metres of the mosque, and they pointed their barrels in the direction of the mosque and started shooting at the mosque, and it was bullet-ridden by these shells from the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The tanks that damaged the mosque, were you able to identify what unit or what army they were from?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, they were tanks belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army. They were olive-green in colour, and they were tanks which we referred to as the 84s, the tank 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you observe these tanks fire upon the mosque?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the date was the 15th of March, which was the last time we were in the area, on the 15th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at that time, the Yugoslav People's Army no longer existed. It had divided into two armies. This particular tank that you saw fire at the mosque, which of the two armies formerly known as the Yugoslav People's Army, did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The tank belonged to the joint forces who were attacking Konjevic Polje, that is to say, the Yugoslav army and the Bosnian Serb forces. They pooled their efforts to attack Konjevic Polje, so it belonged to both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, now, you -- you said that this group of people moved to Srebrenica. Can you tell us the date on which you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I left on the 15th of March, 1993, and the next day, the 16th, I was in the centre of town of Srebrenica, together with all the other people that had come in from the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not counting the 10.000 people that you've told us went to this area, can you approximate for us how many people were in Srebrenica when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in Srebrenica there were at least 40.000 civilians who had congregated there from all occupied territories around Srebrenica, and all of them came to that small space of several kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to briefly describe the living conditions in Srebrenica at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time when I arrived in Srebrenica, quite literally the people were out on the streets. They were lying around, women, children. At every 10 metres somebody had made a fire because it was cold. The weather was cold and people tried to keep warm by making fires. There was not enough room to put up these people anywhere in the buildings because most of the residential buildings had been destroyed anyway. So Srebrenica had no water at that time, no electricity, because the inflow of water and electricity had been cut off by the aggressor forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the period of time when you were in Srebrenica enclave, can you describe for us what knowledge you have with respect to humanitarian convoys destined for Srebrenica and whether or not they were able to reach Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, upon my arrival in Srebrenica, I learnt that before that they had managed to bring in two or three convoys of humanitarian aid. When we arrived on the scene, several more convoys arrived, and two and a half thousand civilians were leaving towards Tuzla. But those convoys, the ones that were supposed to arrive after the demilitisation of Srebrenica, at least once a week, they were stopped by the Serbian forces at Bratunac and Ljubovija and they were not permitted free passage to Srebrenica to bring in the food, clothing, and everything else that the people needed there, because the people were quite literally hungry in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify a point in that last answer. Convoys taking people from Srebrenica out in the direction of Tuzla, were they stopped or were they allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the convoys were stopped, and the aid did not reach Srebrenica. From some other convoys that had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about the outgoing convoys carrying people from Srebrenica to the area of Tuzla. Were those convoys impeded or prevented from leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: As far as those convoys were concerned, outgoing convoys, they were not stopped by the Serb forces. However, the civilians in Srebrenica did stop the convoys because they endeavoured at any price to become part of the convoys and leave Srebrenica. So it was the civilians that stopped the convoys, civilians wanting to flee the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, would I be correct in saying that from April 1993 until the beginning of 1995, that military activity in the area of Srebrenica was at a minimum, compared to what it was at other times?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow that. Military activity by who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: By both forces. I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fighting you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the level of fighting between that period -- or comparing that period to before April 1993 and after the start of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. The fighting was of low intensity. There was hardly any fighting at all, actually, except for a few sporadic incidents that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a change in this at the beginning of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the beginning of 1995, there was constant provocation from the units who held Srebrenica in an encirclement, under siege. Reconnaissance took place every day by the airplanes that flew overhead from the direction of Serbia, and there was systematic preparation for the ultimate and final occupation of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you and a large group of other men in Srebrenica make a decision to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. That happened on the 11th of July, 1995, when there was no saving Srebrenica or the people in it. And we took that decision. We decided to try on that day to break through from Bulja [phoen] towards Tuzla through hostile enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you fear would happen if Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I myself and my fellow fighters were afraid that if we fell into enemy hands we would be liquidated straight away, summarily, without any court or trial. And that's why we decided --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this fear, was it based on any factual event that had occurred prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was precisely our fear that was based on the events that had taken place in April and May 1992, previous events, when the enemy forces of the aggressor from Serbia stormed Bratunac and, without a single bullet having been fired on the Bosnian side, in just the space of a month and a half, about 1.000 civilians were killed, women and children, in Bratunac. And in the Vuk Karadzic school itself, 500 civilians. And we knew very well that if that's the fate they suffered, people who had given no resistance at all, we could only imagine what would happen to us after having fought for three or four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us how many people were in the column of -- that accompanied you.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my rough estimate that the column numbered between 15 -- 12 to 15 thousand men, and it stretched for about 10 to 15 kilometres in its movement towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you -- or I will conclude my questions to you by asking you just to simply look at some photographs which will be displayed on the monitor in front of you. The next one is Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 8. Do you recognise the -- or, I'm sorry, tab 9. Do you recognise what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do recognise this photograph. It is a religious site, a mosque, in fact, that was in Glogova. And it was destroyed and brought into the aspect you see it now between the 9th and 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, sir, I'd ask you to take a look at an exhibit previously tendered. That exhibit is Prosecution Exhibit 440, tab 3. Do you recognise the location depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I do. I recognise this photograph too. Once again, it is a religious site, a mosque, which before the war was situated in Bratunac, the centre of town in fact, and it is no longer in existence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. In the interest of time, I did not work with all of the exhibits. Perhaps at the end of the cross-examination, I could advise the Court which exhibits we would seek to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the cross-examination, I have one question to the Prosecution. If the usher can kindly put two B/C/S versions of tab 8, of this. The English version of this tab, at the end of it, it says ERN number 3134 is a copy of the same document. Put two so that we can see the two pages at the same time. This is the confirmation of war commission by Mr. Karadzic. But if you look at those two pages, the document number, which is handwritten, looks different, and the signature of Mr. Karadzic is different, and the stamp is different. If you help us with that, help us why there should be two versions of the B/C/S version and why Mr. Karadzic signed twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can tell us later, after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. I'd look into the providence of the documents and report to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the usher return. What we'll do is this: We started a quarter of an hour later today, so we'll sit throughout the day a quarter of an hour later. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got a quarter of an hour or so before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just clear up one thing before, Mr. May. This witness was introduced yesterday as a 92 bis witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as you see, in addition to the fact that he was introduced together with all these papers as a 92 bis witness, he was examined, according to your mathematics, for an additional hour and a half. How much time will you give me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was examined for an hour and ten minutes, in fact. We'll take that into account. Just let me consider for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Becirevic, according to the information that you referred to, you in fact convened the Initiative Board for the establishment of the SDA in Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that meeting held in June 1990 in Voljavica in the reading hole of the Podrinje club? Tell me just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Initiative Board, in addition to you and the people you already enumerated, consisted of the chief Imam of the Bratunac community, Mustafa Mujkanovic, as well as Nezid Muratovic, professor of history from Trban [phoen], you said also another man, Semsudin Durakovic, construction engineer, Hasan Smailovic, director of the veterinary station, Safet Dzanic, Mehmetovic, Abid Sirucic, Hasim Ibrahimovic from Bleceva [phoen], Azem Dzanic from Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed a couple of names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I mentioned most of them already in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I make any mistake in listing the names? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: You made a slight mistake in the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about this chief, Imam Mujkanovic? Was he there together with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Speak up, please. How did you fail to mention such a prominent member of the board?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do it deliberately. I may not have recalled him at the moment. There is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know you didn't do it deliberately. Is it true that the founding assembly of the SDA in Bratunac - we were talking about the Initiative Board until now - was held on the 1st September, 1990, nine-zero, at the town stadium, in front of 10.000 people? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's no mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you were the general secretary of the SDA of Bratunac? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were a member of the War Presidency for the Bratunac municipality and that you became president at a meeting held in Konjevic Polje on the 16th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Correct, but it happened only after the crimes committed in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want just yes or no answers in order not to waste time. We'll see about the crimes later. Is it true that you were the president of the War Presidency in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was president of the War Presidency for Konjevic Polje, not Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were the president of the War Presidency personally.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but for Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in 1992 you were personally and very directly involved in the formation of the Patriotic League in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Is it true that the Patriotic League, Patriotic People's League was established in February 1992 at a meeting held at the local commune of Voljavica which you attended and were involved in the work of the Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's true. I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were there when the Patriotic League was formed in February 1992 and you said a moment ago you were not involved in its establishment.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an observer?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I attended more as an observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But also president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in that job at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after the establishment of the Patriotic League, together with Captain Velid Sabic, former officer and deserter from the JNA, you embarked upon the setting up of the Patriotic League for Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were forced to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into what you were forced to do and what you weren't. Serbs too may have been forced to defend themselves but you have another explanation nevertheless. Is it true that that man became chief of staff and you became assistant?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true on the 8th of April, 1992 you transferred all the powers in Konjevic Polje to the so-called Konjevic Polje Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that immediately after the establishment of the Crisis Staff, you set up a group of volunteers which you sent to Kula Grad in Zvornik to fight Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It was only an attempt to help the people who were trying to defend --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Give me just yes or no answers, because you gave an oath here and I heard that you were a lawyer. Is it true you set up a group of volunteers you sent to Kula Grad to fight Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was one of the organisers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One of the organisers. Okay. Is it true that on the 15th of April, 1992 you put yourself at the disposal of the Armed Forces of the BH, Bosnia and Herzegovina? I apologise to the interpreters. I was just warned. I'll repeat my question. Is it true that on the 15th of April, 1992 you put yourself at the orders and service of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that correct, the date?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The date is formally correct, but in actual fact, this happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we have a formal date and an actual date.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It actually happened on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, is it true that as a major of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you occupied the position of assistant commander for morale and religious affairs in the 8th Operative Group of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. I never held that rank in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been put that you were a major. Is that part correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you assistant commander for morale and religious affairs in the 8th Operative Group of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was not assistant commander in the 8th Operative Group. I was assistant commander in a brigade. That's quite a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for what, for religious issues?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: For morale and religious issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you later about what that involves. Were you under the direct command of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't under his direct command. I was under the direct command of Veiz Sabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will give you an exhibit. First of all, I'll read this out, and this is an exhibit, the document I got from the opposite side, numbered 01837194, Opinion and Proposal of the Commander of the 8th Operative Group of Srebrenica. And it says in the document: "Dzemail Becirevic put himself at the disposal of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina as of the 15th of April, 1992." It says "15/4/92." I'm reading "April." "Engaged in the armed forces of the RBH as of the 16th of April, 1992, occupied the position of assistant commander for morale, LPD, and religious issues. He is hereby admitted into active military duty, and I hereby propose that he be promoted into major. He deserves special credit for resisting the enemy together with Veiz Sabic. During the war, he occupied the position of president of the Presidency of -- the War Presidency of Konjevic Polje from July 1992 to January 1993, whereas on the 23rd of January, 1994 he was elected president of the local commune."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's impossible for him to take all that in. Let him look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could also put it on the -- oh, I see Mr. Groome already has it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would also be grateful to have it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have a copy for the interpreters? So much the better, but I suspect we haven't. We've got not a copy for anybody. Just have a look at that, Mr. Becirevic, and tell us about it. Just let the witness see it and then it can be put on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Wait a minute. Can you help us about that document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you help us with that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I put myself at the disposal of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 27th, not the 15th of April, 1992. And as for these positions that I occupied in Konjevic Polje, none of that is in dispute. In Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, go on. In Srebrenica ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Srebrenica, I was assistant commander for morale and religious issues in the 284th East Bosnian Light Brigade, which acted on the axis of Konjevic Polje to Cerska Kamenica. Those were my responsibilities in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the strength of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That brigade had about 1.000 men on paper. Out of that number, one in three or four men had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've already heard similar descriptions. I don't know what you used to kill all those Serbs and raze so many Serb villages to the ground if only one in three or four of you was armed,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Wait a minute. I just want to clarify this document you've shown the witness. What is that document, Mr. Becirevic? Can you help us as to what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, Your Honours, I see this for the very first time. I can see the signature of the commander of the 8th Operative Group, but I don't remember that I personally proposed myself for promotion into whatever rank. I was, by rank, senior lieutenant, and in order to be promoted, I either had to apply first or somebody had to propose me for promotion into major.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Since this is a document of their 8th Operative Group signed by Naser Oric, I think it can be admitted as an exhibit, unless you absolutely refuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit that as an exhibit. If the usher would like to go and get it, yes. Give it the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be 131, in my calculation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour. Defence Exhibit 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This morning, in this abbreviated examination-in-chief, but also on page 6 in paragraph 5 of your statement, you describe how on the 17th of April, 1992 outside Fontana Hotel in Bratunac you saw some "Arkan's men, Seselj's men wearing special uniforms --" I'm reading from your statement. Let me look up this page 6 of your statement because -- "I saw three soldiers outside the entrance, their guns at the ready, wearing special uniforms, bandannas," and so on. How come you're saying today, since you claim you saw some paramilitaries, how do you know who they were and how come you are mentioning JNA as well today, which is not in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the statement be put before the witness. He does identify the members of that paramilitary group in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give the number of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is paragraph 20 on the numbered version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness find his way around. You can't let him not deal with matters which you put to him. Do you see that, Mr. Becirevic? Have you got the point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Keep the statement there. We're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Becirevic, in this adjournment and any others there may be during your evidence, would you remember not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one thing. In your statement, you mentioned what I read out to you, that is to say, on page 6, 17th of April, a group of Arkan's men arrived in Bratunac from Serbia. "They entered the hotel and took it over. I saw three soldiers outside the front door holding their weapons at the ready. They had special uniforms which I recognised from television reports, they wore a special bandana around their heads," and so on and so forth, "but I'm sure they were from Arkan's group." You don't mention the JNA here. You don't mention Seselj's men at all. You now mention the JNA, Seselj's men, Arkan's men, even the Red Berets. And here you talk about bandannas around their heads. Did you invent all of this?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not invent anything. I was in Bratunac on that day, and I saw these paramilitary formations that had come from Serbia with different uniforms and insignia that they had on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Becirevic, that even the Serb volunteer guard, Arkan's guard, was not in Bratunac at all? It was some group of criminals from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not correct, because all of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina watched television and saw what Arkan's men did in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Bratunac. You're talking about Bratunac, not Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: But such groups entered Bratunac on the 17th of April as well and occupied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying such groups or those groups?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Groups that wore the same uniform and the same insignia. Those that took Bijeljina were in Bratunac on the 17th of April, 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Do you know who Nijaz Masic is?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Nijaz Masic. He's a professor who worked at the high school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. He wrote a book that is entitled "The Truth About Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that he wrote that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You knew him personally, I assume. You know him personally?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I do know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the book, he says, as a matter of fact, that some commission had been set up of the War Presidency of the Municipality of Bratunac with its seat in Srebrenica consisting of the following persons: Dzemail Becirevic, Selmo Ibisevic and Nijaz Masic. So together with you he was a member of this commission consisting of three members.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of war commission you're talking about. This was a commission that had as its objective to get out of Srebrenica and to reach Tuzla. However, it never succeeded in this intention of theirs because in the first attempt made to that effect the Serb forces ambushed them and they had to return and people were even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't finish that job, but I just wanted to establish your immediate connection to Nijaz Masic, the work you did together. Now, since you've mentioned all of this, everything you saw on the 17th of April, now let us leave aside the differences concerning what it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. says -- between what you said here and what it says in the statement. Give me a precise answer to the following question: Is it correct that on the 17th of April, 1992 you were not in Bratunac at all or in Hrncici and that therefore you could not see either Arkan's men or Seselj's men or soldiers or anybody else or anything else. You could not feel endangered in any way at all because you were not in Bratunac on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the truth is that on the 17th of April, 1992 I was in Bratunac. There are witnesses as to who I came to Bratunac with and who I returned with, and there are also Serbs who I found in my office, one of my clerks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Becirevic. I'm going to read a paragraph from page 65 of Nijaz Masic's book, in which it says quite literally --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this has been marked by 02060087, 65, page 65 of the book, that is. I am going to read this paragraph. "In the night between the 27th and 28th of April, 1992, with Aganovic Brdo there was a new meeting of armed prominent persons from Konjevic Polje. At this meeting the citizens of Konjevic Polje were familiarised with the demand made --" Am I reading too fast for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At the meeting the citizens of Konjevic Polje were familiarised with the demand made by the Chetniks and their following intentions. A decision was reached to establish contact with Cerska as soon as possible and to prevent the surrender of weapons in that area and in this way create a united front against the aggressor."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, pay attention to the following sentence. I'm not omitting anything: "Velid Sabic and Dzemail Becirevic familiarised the persons present with their visit -- their travel made on the 17th of April, 1992 to Tuzla, where they were received by Fuad Hadziabdic and he said to them that he could not help them with arming along with the recommendation," et cetera, et cetera. And then it comes to the following page. So at that meeting you told people about your trip, about your travel to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer these passages, if you're going to put them to him. What is suggested by this author, as you've heard, Mr. Becirevic, is that you, on the 17th of April, travelled to Tuzla to try and get help. Is the author right about that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am going to answer this question. On the 17th of April, I was in Bratunac until 12.00. When I saw what was going on in Bratunac, that Bratunac would be occupied, from Bratunac I made a telephone call to my superior, Fuad Hadziabdic, and I asked him what to do. I said some military people came here, some paramilitary forces, they've occupied the town, it's almost fallen into their hands. And he answered me, quite literally, "Over the telephone I cannot give you any kind of answer or assistance. Therefore, try to come with Velid Sabic --" because I told him that Velid Sabic was there too. And he said, come with him to Tuzla and we are going to agree on all of this. And then at 12.00 I left Bratunac. I came to Konjevic Polje. Around 1500 hours, we set out for Tuzla. We arrived in Tuzla. We met only for about 15 minutes with this Fuad. He was the Assistant Minister for National Defence for the Tuzla region. He can confirm that. He said to us that he could not help us, he could not help Bratunac and the people of Bratunac. He said that Tuzla was in danger as well and that Tuzla needed help too. He said, "Go back there. Go back to these people in Konjevic Polje. Let the army leave. Try to engage in partisan warfare when the time comes. Until the army leaves, you cannot take any kind of action." So around 1700 hours, we returned. There are witnesses. There is a lawyer, Salcin Dzamic, who we found in Tuzla and who asked us, "Where are you going back to? Do you know that Bratunac fell today at 3.00?" We said we had been in Bratunac until 12.00. "But never mind. We're going back there again because the people are waiting for us there. We are going to help the people." So in the evening we returned to Konjevic Polje. That is the truth. And I have hundreds of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it is not being contested that on the 17th of April, 1992 you and Velid Sabic went to Tuzla and that you were received there by Fuad Hadziabdic and he said that he could not help you and all of this happened at this lightning speed that you've referred to. And how far is the distance between Bratunac and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell the Honourable Trial Chamber that from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje it takes about 20 minutes by car, and from Konjevic Polje to Tuzla we went along the following road: Milici, where we were stopped by the Serb police, and they searched us, and then we went via Vlasenica, Tisce, Kladanj, we reached Tuzla. We were down there for about half an hour or an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long does one travel from Bratunac via Konjevic Polje, Kladanj, and so on, all these places you mentioned, to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: About an hour and a half or two by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
