utterances.text: So you need two hours to arrive in Tuzla without anybody detaining you along the way, and you had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we were just searched at two checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you did all of that within this short span of time that you described.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, could you please take this page, which is marked by this number of the opposite side, would you please take it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I doubt if it's evidence because it's what somebody has written in a book. So I doubt it's evidence. But let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he confirmed what it says in the book. That is precisely what I'm saying, that on that day he was in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have hundreds of witnesses who are going to confirm that on that day I was in Bratunac until 12.00, that I was in my office, that Gavric, my clerk, saw me and said to me, "What are you waiting for here? Run away. See that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're not going to admit that page. You've heard what the witness says about it. In fact, there doesn't seem to be much dispute about what you allege. He says he went to Tuzla that afternoon but was in Bratunac in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it's not disputed that during the night between the 27th and 28th of April at this meeting at Aganovic Brdo, together with a few armed men from Konjevic Polje, that you told them about your trip to Tuzla on the 17th and the meeting with Hadziabdic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It is not disputed that on the 27th in the evening we were at Aganovic Brdo, and it is quite clear why we met there; because we were expelled from our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Am I right further on when I say that you established the 114th East Bosnian Brigade from Konjevic Polje, which became a part of the 284th East Bosnian Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It is correct, Your Honours, that I am one of the participants, and that the commander of that brigade was a former officer of the Yugoslav army Sabic Velid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that you were within the command of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I was assistant commander for morale in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The command of this unit consisted of the following persons, as it says on page 101 of this book, and it also has been marked by the other side as 06260106, was Velid Sabic, commander; then Suljic, deputy; Ejub Dedic, chief of staff; Fehim Hasanovic; Ismet Celikovic; Nail Jusupovic; Mehmedalija Mehic; Fadil Muminovic; Fadil Dedic; Dzemail Becirevic - you, that is - Enes Ibrahimovic; Ismet Mujanovic; Hajrudin Turnadzic; and Avdo Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't be expected to take all these names in. Did you get those names and is it right that they were -- formed part of the brigade, or would you like any of them repeated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no need. I know most of these people, and they were in the brigade, 284 EB Srebrenica, and I was one of the members too, of course, of this top command of this brigade in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is what I -- what I described as the top command of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, do you know, Mr. Becirevic, that the State Commission for War Crimes and Genocide of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in its memorandum on war crimes and genocide in Eastern Bosnia, the municipalities of Bratunac, Skelani, and Srebrenica, dated the month of April 1993, you were -- put you on the list as one of the organisers of the genocide against the Serb people under the column of "Officials and Organisers"?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. But Dzemail Becirevic has a well-known address. Right now I live in Sarajevo. I often travel to Bratunac. I am an Assemblyman in the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac, and that kind of question was put to me in 1997, when I was a candidate for vice-president of the Assembly and I was told that allegedly I had committed some kind of war crimes, and then the international community said to these persons who had raised this question that they should present evidence to that effect, and they were given a deadline, a 30-day deadline. If they have anything to say against me, they could go ahead. Since then it's been six years, and I am still at everybody's disposal. My address is well-known. If they have anything, let them go ahead with it, but they have to prove it. I have been called here first and foremost to testify about the aggression that had been carried out against Bosnia-Herzegovina, namely, the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, lest you interrupt me in my efforts to indicate by way of questions what crimes were committed and the number of victims and also how many villages were razed to the ground and torched in the municipality of Bratunac, I wish to tender into evidence this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have indicated that particular document several times in its entirety. I wish to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, which is the document that you're asking to admit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The memorandum about war crimes and the crime of genocide in Eastern Bosnia in the municipalities of Bratunac, Skelani, and Srebrenica committed against the Serb people from April 1992 until April 1993. This was compiled by the Yugoslav State Committee for War Crimes and Genocide, and the date is April 1993. On this page, which the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I suppose one course, Mr. Groome - I mean, maybe you have an objection - may be to mark it for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not oppose marking it for identification. I would object, on behalf of the Prosecution, to its introduction in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would seem reasonable to mark it for identification. Yes, we will do that and get a number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 132, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before you mark it for identification, I would just like to inform you that the title page of the document is 01975, and it is the number provided by the opposite side. The page is the one I mentioned to Mr. Becirevic, and it is 00678851, and the title there is "A list of war criminals in the territory of Bratunac, Srebrenica, Milici, Vlasenica, and Skelani for which evidence and proof exists that they are in Srebrenica." And under number 14, we find the name of Becirevic Dzemail, born in 1960 in Bratunac. So here you have the document in its entirety for you to see for yourselves. As the opposite side does have this document, I assume that it has certain responsibilities with respect to those war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is another one of several commissions funded and organised by respected members of the conflict that investigated crimes during the war and issued these reports. Just as the Prosecution has never sought to admit the results of these commissions as evidence of -- that Mr. Milosevic is guilty of war crimes, the Prosecution opposes that they're introduced as evidence of that somebody else has committed any crimes. The Prosecution received these reports from respective members of the party. In light of our obligations under Rule 68, a full copy of that was provided to the accused so that he could use it in his questioning of the witness. But it's the Prosecution's position that these documents in and of themselves do not bear sufficient reliability or credibility to be introduced into evidence for the proof of the facts that they assert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, at this stage the exhibit will be simply marked for identification purposes. If in due course evidence is produced to support it, then of course we'll reconsider whether it should be introduced fully or not. Let me hand it back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have an excerpt from the criminal files of those accused of war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 to 1995. I've extracted page 76 from that document, and it includes a number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll just read out what has to do with you, Mr. Becirevic, and that is this: It says: "Becirevic Dzemail, born in 1960 in Bratunac, secretary of the SDA in Bratunac, responsible for preparing to attack military formations in Bratunac against the civilian population of Serbian villages and settlements -- Bratunac settlement, Konjevic Polje, and others. And between May and December 1992 a mass and individual killings and took place of civilians, including women, children, elderly persons, sick people, disabled people, and so on. And most of the houses and villages were then looted, burnt to the ground, or destroyed. In the course of these attacks, without any military need, the civilian population was mistreated, massacred, and tortured, taken off to prisons and camps, and displaced in the efforts of ethnic cleansing of the area." So these are all excerpts from criminal files against the perpetrators of war crimes committed against the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I've just read out this brief extract, which indicates that this took place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- and mentions the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the document, and then he can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer. Who is it who makes these allegations, Mr. Milosevic? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says there, the heading, it is "The excerpt from criminal files by the organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina," or rather, I suppose that they are the authorities -- the competent authorities in the area -- in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] now, Mr. Becirevic, you can look at that document -- You could look at that document and see what it says. You can comment upon the document, and you can also deal with the allegation that you took part in organising attacks on villages which resulted in them being razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the allegations made by the accused are absolutely not true. First of all, I have been called here to testify about the organisation, aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, in specific terms the Bratunac municipality, the aggression itself and the genocide that was committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know why you've come here and what you've said, so there's no need to repeat that. But obviously these allegations are being made and you should have a chance to deal with them. Is there a word of truth in anything that's written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is not a word of truth in all this, because at that material time I was in Konjevic Polje and Konjevic Polje exclusively waged defensive operations. That is to say, there were daily attacks launched against it precisely from the opposite side, so how could we attack somebody when we were actually under a total encirclement and siege from the 17th of April right up to the time we were expelled towards Srebrenica. Konjevic Polje had no exits anywhere. So this is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Groome, again, marked for identification, unless you have any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to quite specific and concrete questions, Mr. Becirevic, but tell me first this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. We're just going to have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 133, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that you personally were involved in the activities to arm, train, and form the Muslim military commands and units in the villages of Sandici, Locici, Urkovici, Pervani, Kamenica, Pobrdje and Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct that those villages are the most populous and largest part of the Bratunac municipality in which 99 per cent of the population are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The local community of Konjevic Polje before the war, according to the population census, numbered 5.600 inhabitants and it was one of the largest local communities in the Bratunac municipality. The only local community, in fact, which offered an organised -- organised defence to the aggressor. All the other local communities where the Muslim people were in the majority, in the space of one and a half months, were razed to the ground. That is to say, ethnic cleansing took place and during that one and a half months about 1.000 women and children were killed, and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've already said that. What I'm asking you is this -- would you please answer my question. There's no need to repeat your testimony, which does not relate to my question. So you were the head of the Wartime Presidency in Konjevic Polje but you say -- yet you say that you were not the organiser of the activities to train and establish Muslim military commands in those villages. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I'm claiming that I did not take part in any kind of training because I was an ordinary soldier in the former JNA, so that I am not a military expert in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about organisation. I'm not saying that you trained them and showed them how to assemble or disassemble a rifle or anything like that or hold rifle practice. But another question: Is it true that it was precisely you, together with this man Rahid Sabic, who brought Nurif Rizvanovic to those parts who was also a former officer and in fact deserter of the JNA who was otherwise a native of Glogova. You brought him exclusively in order to implement military training and attack the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's not true. We were not able to bring him in at all. What we could say is that you probably slipped him into the area, because he arrived in the month of August and he came from Tuzla with a unit to the Konjevic Polje area. Part of the unit stayed on in Konjevic Polje, whereas the rest of the unit went on to Srebrenica. So how could we have brought him in? We were under a total siege, so how would we bring in anybody from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean what you want to say that the Serbs brought him, this Rizvanovic, who brought with him 500 soldiers from all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: They let him pass through. They let him pass over 100 kilometres of Serb territory to arrive in Konjevic Polje. I don't know what their aim in doing that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as of 1992, together with you and all the rest, he was very prominent in perpetrating war crimes and genocide against the Serbian population there, precisely this man called Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he didn't fight in Konjevic Polje and commit war crimes against Serbian civilians in that whole encirclement?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: He came to help his own people because he originated from Glogova and it was his aim to go back to his native region and help the people of Glogova. That was what he wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said he was from Glogova. And is it true that this man Rizvanovic, due to the power fight, clashed with Naser Oric who later liquidated him, precisely in this clash and power struggle that they had? And I'm talking about the Muslim forces in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: As to the details of this alleged clash between them, power struggle between them, I don't know. But Nurif Rizvanovic, when he left for Srebrenica, lost his life at the enemy lines, that is to say, the Serb front. Now, how he lost his life, I really can't say. I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know the details, I won't pursue the issue. But tell me this: Before the conflict in the Bratunac municipality, you were the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence in Bratunac municipality. And that is what it says on page 2 of your statement, paragraph 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 4 of your statement, you speak about arming the Territorial Defence of Bratunac and the weapons they had; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take a look. What page and paragraph did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 4 of your statement speaks about arming the Territorial Defence of Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I speak about how the weapons were taken over from the Territorial Defence of Bratunac by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in 1989 those weapons were removed. Did I follow you correctly? So you were talking about the year 1989 when the weapons were transferred from Bratunac. Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army collected up all the weapons and took it across the bridge, the Ljubovija bridge into Serbia. Where the weapons ended up, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the JNA in 1989 was throughout the territory of the SFRY, Bratunac, Ljubovija, and any other place because it was within the borders of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything. I just said that they collected up all the weapons and took it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence in 1989?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I told you where I was at the time and where I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then you must know, even if you weren't in that position, you must have known that something like that -- you could have been aware only in 1990 when the Federal Presidency decided to displace the arms from the Territorial Defence to store it in the JNA barracks and depots. The Federal Assembly in full composition in 1990 made that decision, and you must have known about it. That is, to transfer the TO weapons to the JNA barracks and depots because it was safer and more secure there. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: We knew that a decision of that kind was taken and that the weapons were collected up in Bratunac. I know that because I saw it with my own eyes. I saw the weapons being taken away. So that is not being contested. You're denying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it. I'm asking you on the basis of my information, Mr. Becirevic. You worked as the defence secretary. I assume you were aware of a decision taken by the Presidency of Yugoslavia according to which the weapons of the Territorial Defence should be placed under you -- JNA warehouse protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that. Move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say that the weapons were supposed to be transferred to the barracks of the Tuzla Corps but that the trucks in fact took the direction of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I just said that during that period of time I was working in a socially owned company and that I was only 50 metres away from that particular place and that I was 10 metres away from the trucks when they loaded up the weapons and took them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Were you an escort for that weapons transport?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No. Why would I have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know the weapons weren't taken to Tuzla but somewhere to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: They took the direction of Ljubovija. Where it ended up, I don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're in fact saying -- you in fact say on that same page that there was a barracks in Ljubovija. You talk about that particular barracks; right? Have you ever been to the Ljubovija barracks?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I've never been to the Ljubovija barracks but I just said that the weapons were taken in the direction of Ljubovija, towards Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that you don't know what kind of unit was stationed there at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I said that there was a barracks there and that it was common knowledge that it was JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the only army that existed in the SFRY, as far as I know, so that's no secret.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a secret, and it's not being contested either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know what kind of unit this was nor what type and quantity of ammunition the unit had at its disposal or anything about its strength. Am I right when I say that? That particular unit in Ljubovija, that's the one that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there, so I couldn't know what kind of unit it was, how many men it numbered, but what I did see was that it was from the positions at Ljubovija, and I'm talking about 1991, that the barrels were turned and pointed towards Bratunac, and that was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll clear that up in due course. Now, as you say you know nothing about the unit, how come you say that in the barracks in 1991 a tank unit arrived of some kind, and prior to that you say that you know nothing about the unit or its weapons?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: What I'm telling you is this: I saw with my very own eyes that the tanks, their barrels, were turned towards --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that some unit arrived. How can you know that the tanks weren't there beforehand at the Ljubovija barracks, already in place? Because you say a tank unit turned up in 1991. How do you know they weren't already there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, reinforcements were sent from other areas to the territory of Ljubovija. And once again, as I say, their barrels were turned towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've shown us some documents here and you speak about the establishment of the Serbian Municipality of Bratunac. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that their barrels were pointed to some forces in Ljubovija -- or rather, that the Yugoslav People's Army's barrels were turned to Bratunac. And you say that the JNA assisted the Serbs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, in December of that year, the Serb Municipality of Bratunac was established, although the legal municipality of Bratunac was already in existence. A government was set up, a Serb government, although Bratunac already had the executive board of its own legal government. So all the preparations had been concluded on the part of the Serbs in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Becirevic, the preparations that were completed and so on, I'm not asking you that now. You mentioned tanks, you mentioned Howitzers, you mentioned their barrels being turned towards Bratunac. Did those Howitzers and tanks shoot at the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and in the spring of 1992, they did not open fire. But it was sufficient for the people to see their barrels turned towards Bratunac and the area around Bratunac. This instilled fear in the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this explanation that there was some deployment of JNA forces in the barracks in Ljubovija, which had existed for decades there, your explanation is to instil fear in the population. But you say they did not shoot. So all those tanks and barrels were never used. They never opened fire towards the Bratunac municipality. Did they open fire across the Drina River at all?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not. But it was enough for their barrels to be turned towards Bratunac. That was a clear indication of what was in store for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As we have Serbs and Muslims living in Bratunac, then both these ethnic groups must have been afraid of the gun barrels pointed at them. I don't think a shell can choose what ethnic group it's going to shoot at.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you didn't say they opened fire, let us not dwell on it. Tell me one thing: On page 3, paragraph 8, you explained that Bratunac, according to the census in 1991, had 33.500 inhabitants. Out of that, 11.300 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that according to the census in 1991, there were 33.500 inhabitants in Bratunac, out of which 64 per cent Bosnians, 33 per cent Serbs, and the rest were others. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the figure from the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 2, paragraph 5, you say that in end 1989 you started feeling tensions and that you - I suppose that means Muslims - Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. started hearing Serb propaganda about Serbs being driven out, but you say that the real truth was that people were leaving Bratunac in search for jobs. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an indisputable fact that there was an attempt by the Serbian propaganda to present it as Serbs leaving Bratunac under pressure, under duress, but later events showed that they were in fact leaving for economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that they were leaving in order to look for jobs elsewhere. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, in the third paragraph, you say, "But Serbs held leading and managerial positions."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I meant public enterprises, about 20 of them that existed in Bratunac. And all the major posts, in fact 80 per cent of them, were held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've heard that before. You say that members of the Serb community, which was twice smaller than the Muslim community, held all the managerial positions and that Serbs were not being driven out. They were, rather, leaving in order to look for jobs elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I meant public enterprises where key positions were held by Serbs in 80 per cent of all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are a law graduate and you worked in the municipal administration. Do you know that, for instance, in the 1931 census 50 per cent of the population were Serbs in Bratunac, Muslims were a minority?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I do not know this piece of information. In 1991, I was in the commission for the census and that is why I quoted that information. What was the case 50 years ago, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware that immediately after the Second World War, for reasons which this Tribunal does not find interesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 51, so he's not going to do the Second World War. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know. And I was just going to say that these are the reasons which do not meet with your interest. But I suppose that Mr. Becirevic, who says he is a law graduate, knows that in 1959, after Serbs returned to the lands from which they were driven out, their number rose to over 50 per cent of the total population in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with that. He says he doesn't know about these figures, and I don't see what the relevance of them is. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, from 50 per cent, over that period, their number dropped to 30 per cent but Serbs held all the key positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who is Sead Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he was the director of Vihor enterprise?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I'll be happy to answer this question. We are talking about socially owned enterprises which have to be distinguished from private enterprises. You are a lawyer, just as I am by education, and you must know that in socially owned enterprises such as Vihor was, it was the workers who decided who the director would be. There were both Serbs and Muslims in those posts, but only the most capable people remained, those who were able to make sure that workers got their wages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking you to confirm this data, nothing else, because we have heard talk about some sort of discrimination against Muslims. Okay. He was director of Vihor. Was Fahro Djordjic director of the Kaolin factory?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that it was workers who put these people in those positions, because they managed to provide their wages from month to month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you who appointed them, the workers' council or somebody else. I'm just asking you: Were these people indeed directors of those enterprises?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: They were, but they were only because they were capable people who ensured wages for both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure they were. That's not what we are discussing. Was Mujo Mujicic the director of the ceramics factory? Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: My answer is the same. Yes; the workers decided it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Edo Ahmic director of the cardboard factory?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about public enterprises. And if you want to insist, that was the ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm also talking about socially owned enterprises. Kaolin factory, the cardboard factory, all of them were socially owned. Was Cazim Avdic director of Feros?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That was in Srebrenica, I don't want to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Enver Hekic director of the Autotransport hauling enterprise?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Rifat Besic, was he director of the timber factory in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: You are referring to enterprises which I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a war crimes trial on which immensely serious charges are brought. Does it matter who was in charge of the cardboard factory? What does it matter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it matters precisely because it is insinuated here that there was some sort of discrimination against Muslims, and I took the trouble of looking up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But you could put it shortly. We don't need this kind of detail. You see -- I mean, are you saying that there was discrimination against Muslims in Bratunac before the conflict broke out? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as public enterprises are concerned, yes, there was. And here is an example: Out of four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you to try and shorten this. Is it true, as the accused has put, that there were Muslims who were in charge of these enterprises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, talking about socially owned enterprises, I answered this question. But there was discrimination in public enterprises, where all the key positions were held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you call public enterprises? You mean the street sweeping service.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Let me answer. There were two banks in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why would bank be a public enterprise and a mine isn't?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The mine is in Srebrenica. Let us take the social accounting service, the post office, the four key public enterprises, the SDK, the social accountancy service through which all funds were transferred. All these positions were held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it matter who was the director of the post office, Serb or Muslim? Since I enumerated these, I can enumerate more enterprises in Bratunac, not just a few, as Mr. May puts it, but almost all of them managed by Muslims. What kind of managerial or other domination of Serbs in Bratunac are you talking about? Is it true that the majority of general managers in Bratunac were Muslims, an overwhelming majority?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. And I have already answered. I am talking here about public companies. There were about 20 of them. And we Muslims demanded that they be split half/half after the elections in 1990, and we never managed to get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Becirevic. I know, and I understand your demand, but I considered it as an absolutely unprincipled thing. Is it true that Nijaz Dubicic was president of the municipal administration in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's true, but it's also true that Radoljub Djukanovic was president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you who the president of the municipality was. I'm not asking about the executive board. And you are answering me yes, but the other one was president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That was according to the electoral results.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was a Muslim. Was Senad Hadzic chief of police in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: His name is Senad Hodzic. But the commander was, again, Mandic Nikola.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're answering me again that the commander was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Because that's how it was. One was Serb, one was Muslim, the chief and deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was that in Kravica you were telling me about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: In Stajici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And both key people in the police were replaced after that incident, both the Serb and the Muslim.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So president of the police, chief of the SUP, head of the municipal administration for -- municipal section for civil defence and protection. You were the secretary, is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It boils down to the same thing. Is it true that the chief of the staff for National Defence was Sead Mujicic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you: The executive board consisted of three Muslims and three Serbs. Can you imagine how they operated? It was consistently obstructed. Why? Because of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously it was the SDS which is to blame for everything and the SDA is not to blame for anything. All right. Tell me now: Is it true that you in fact made up this domination of Serbs in managerial positions?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't make anything up; It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I read you a list of Muslim names, people who were managers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've now exhausted this topic. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Is it true that you made up also the economic reasons for which Serbs left Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't make it up. There was a conference held, attended by a thousand citizens, both Serbs and Muslims, which noted and concluded that there is no emigration of Serbs under pressure. All the emigration was due to other reasons. Every second house in my own place, Konjevic Polje, has men working in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they went for economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It was not the Muslims who expelled them, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say in your statement, "From the Party of Democratic Action, we tried to make certain decisions such as decisions to replace directors of certain public enterprises because all of them were Serbs after the elections." That means you decided to replace people because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: We were not in a position to make such decisions. It was up to the Municipal Assembly to decide. But since the Municipal Assembly had its work completely blocked, not a single decision it made after its establishment could pass without the approval of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am just quoting. Those are the last lines on page 3: "In the course of the meetings that followed, we in the SDA tried to make some decisions such as to change some of the managers of public enterprises in town because they were all Serbs." You tell me now that you were not making such decisions. Why did you want to replace them? Because they were no good or because they were Serbs? You told me that the only criterion for being a general manager was ability and skill, and in the same breath you tell me here in the statement that you wanted to replace them because they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It was not up to us, in any case. The Assembly was to decide on that. But the Serbs did not like it. They wanted their situation to remain on status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was their main deficiency that they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, we're not talking about the skill of a person - for instance, director of the SDK - if that man gave all the funds to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can a director of a section for payment transactions give funds to somebody to whom these funds are not due?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That, unfortunately, did happen in the beginning of 1992, and documents clearly show that people who paid contributions into their pension funds, as was established after the war, had these funds diverted. These funds never reached Tuzla, where they were supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have no evidence of who stole money from a branch of the SDK. This is a totally different issue. We have many other issues to discuss and time is short. If there was a thief who stole the money, it's a completely different matter. You say that the tensions grew more intense when Serbs who passed on buses through Bratunac put up my pictures in the windows.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's true. That was the case with all vehicles coming from the direction of Ljubovija. Your photograph was in the windows of all vehicles, and that caused discontent among Muslims. Some windows were shattered and so on. There were incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You followed the newspapers, I suppose, since you are a lawyer, didn't you? Are you aware that I made statements in newspapers, and I may have been the only politician in Yugoslavia at the time who publicly asked that his photograph not be put up anywhere because those times were already past and new times prevailed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I never read anything of the sort. All I know is that your pictures were put up in Bratunac on all public buildings, institutions, in offices, whereas you were not head of state in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I was not. I'm not claiming otherwise. You say on page 3, paragraph 2 that the Serbian Democratic Party in Bratunac was set up in November 1990; is that so? Doesn't that show -- since we were trying to establish a moment ago when the SDA was set up, doesn't this show that the SDS was established five months later, after the establishment of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. What is referred to here are founding assembly meetings. The SDA founding assembly was on the 1st of September, 1990, and the SDS founding assembly followed immediately. The initiatives for setting up the party were in May or June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only reading what you wrote on page 3, paragraph 2: "The SDS party was organised in Bratunac in October or November 1990."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: You mean the founding assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Five months after the establishment of SDA. We have dates for both parties, and the difference is five months.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That is not so. You misunderstood. This is about a founding assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you attended the founding assembly meeting of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you only remember part of the speech held by Velibor Ostojic, who claimed that Muslims in Bosnia had a plan to connect Bosnia with Sandzak, Sandzak being a part of Serbia; isn't that so? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What is in dispute here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you did not put up your own proposal for linking up with Sandzak? Do you know that the Patriotic People's League, which you must know, having been their official, had staffs for the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including one for Sandzak and one for Kosovo, although Sandzak and Kosovo are parts of Serbia? Are these facts correct or not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: They're partly correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, partly correct. Now, tell me, since you and some other witnesses explained that actually Arkan, with his 25 men who came to Bijeljina, carried out an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, let's leave it aside. I mean, if that is a state, that 25 men can carry out an aggression against, let's leave that aside. But do you know how many Muslims, how many thousands of Muslims from Sandzak fought in the ranks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these figures, how many people from Sandzak came to fight on the side of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they sent by some kind of government from Serbia to be volunteers in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the witness's evidence. Now, let's move on to another topic, which is...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of the statement, you say that on the 27th of August, 1991 you personally, as secretary for the Secretariat for National Defence, hid the military conscript's records, put them away in a safe place. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I acted upon instructions of the Ministry of Defence from Sarajevo because we received information that the Yugoslav People's Army would come to seize these records from the secretariat by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these records were supposed to be taken over by the army according to a decision passed by the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct, because I would have had to receive such an order. It would have had to come to my desk or to the desk of the president of the municipality or the president of the executive council. One of the three of us would have had to receive such an order, but we never did receive any such order. It was only the members of the Crisis Staff of the SDS came to my office and asked me by way of an ultimatum that I hand them over these records and it's only natural that I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. One at a time, please. You must remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, you were telling Muslims not to respond to call-ups, military call-ups.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but that was in 1991, when the war in Croatia was on, and I knew that these young men were being sent to the front line in Croatia. I knew that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were head of the Secretariat for National Defence and you didn't want people to go into the army and so on and so forth. So you obstructed your very own work, didn't you? If you were warning Muslims not to answer the call-up, why didn't you warn the Serbs too not to answer the call-up?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, Your Honours, it was the Crisis Staff of the SDS that came to me and asked me by way of ultimatum to hand over the records, and they said to me, "If you Muslims don't want to wage war in Croatia, give me the records of the Serbs. They want to wage war and they want to carry out mobilisation." I could not meet such a request of the SDS Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But at the same time, you present this activity of yours as some kind of anti-war obstruction of mobilisation and hiding military records; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: My objective was precisely that these innocent young men do not go to fight the war in Croatia, so I stand by the fact that I acted upon instructions of the Ministry of Defence. So my objective was to stop this mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. These were the instructions of the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But at the same time, you worked on arming the Muslim population of Bratunac; is that right, Mr. Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, here is a document for you. It is the centre of public security from Tuzla, that is to say, Bosnia-Herzegovina, where it says: "0303-766. By way of operative work in the field, on the 31st of August and on the 1st of September this year, that is to say, 1991, we have received several pieces of information." So you see, this is 1991. There is no war; there is no conflict; there is no nothing. This is mid-1991. "We received several pieces of information which indicate that in the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica there is an increasingly present illegal procurement and distribution of weapons and ammunition as well as the spreading of rumours, misinformation, disturbing the public law and order, setting up armed patrols and barricades. We have been informed by our sources Dzanic Azem, member of the Party of Democratic Action in Bratunac, together with Becirevic Dzemail, secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence of Bratunac, a certain Safet, director of the veterinary station in Bratunac, with the knowledge of Kavazbasic Mirsad, president of the municipal committee of the Party of Democratic Action, Munisovic Nezir [phoen], head of the public security station in Bratunac, and other members of the leadership of this party used an official car, licence number ZV - that's Zvornik - 26200, owned by the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence of Bratunac is bringing weapons in from Sarajevo and then they are taking over these weapons from the headquarters of the Party of Democratic Action and distributing these weapons to persons of Muslim ethnicity in the territory of this municipality. So two months ago --" I don't know "24 pistols were transferred in this way, and later they were sold at a price of 15.000 dinars per piece. And then a number of persons, together with Sead Hadziabdic, owner of the Royal Restaurant, sold these weapons to Dzanic, yet another Dzanic, a Muslim, at the price of 1.500 Deutschmark in Drinjaca, municipality of Zvornik." Now, this is illegible, with a person nicknamed Taran in Konjevic Polje, a restaurant owner, also Abdic Nezad and Siranovic [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You can't just read out documents at great length. The witness is giving evidence and he must be able to deal with them. It's alleged, you see, in this document, and we'll hear where the accused got it from, but it's alleged that you, in September 1991, were introducing weapons into Bratunac from Sarajevo and distributing them. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no truth in this. From Sarajevo to Bratunac is about 145 kilometres. Imagine someone going into that kind of thing, transporting weapons from Sarajevo, where there are dozens of police patrols along the way. And whoever would transport this would be arrested, and nobody would allow oneself to do such a thing. And imagine using a small Yugo car for that. This is a small car. I never did any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it usually is done. Civilian cars, things like that. This was a vehicle of your secretariat, and this is a document of the public security centre of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, please, I would like to have it admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just want to say if this was their report, why didn't they stop this? Why didn't they stop this delivery? Why didn't they show the evidence and proof? These are pure insinuations. This has nothing to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him have a look. Let him have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Read it. It's all there, and it's all nicely highlighted, all the things I asked you about. Since I am giving you the document in its entirety, you can read everything that it says.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: So I answered this question. There's no truth in this, no truth whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Groome, marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this a document which the Prosecution handed over, in fact, or is it one the accused --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was one that was handed over by the Prosecution, but I have no idea of its providence. I could investigate that for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it out exactly as it stands, Mr. May. And since there is a translation of this document, you can compare, and it's theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give it a number marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 134, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Becirevic, do you continue to claim that in the summer of 1991 you were not involved in the illegal arming of Muslims in the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It is not correct that I was involved in such efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that this entire farce, with the theft and concealing of military records on the 27th of August was not anti-war but it was simply aimed at opening up a new front in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. On our part, we who hid this -- these military records, we said what our objective was. And the objective of the Crisis Staff of the SDS was completely contrary to that. I spoke about that. I really don't want to go into it any further. If necessary, I can go into the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirevic, since you were assistant commander for religious affairs, did you read the Islamic declaration? Have you read the Islamic declaration of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't. And as far as religious affairs are concerned, religious matters, within my field of work I had a man who was strictly in charge of that. But I dealt with other matters in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This obstruction of carrying out the functions -- or rather, this hiding of records and this arming of Muslims, wasn't all of that assistance to the spectre of the Ustasha movement that rose in Croatia and it is with their assistance that you actually did what you did to the Serb minority in Bratunac and in this way you ensured your supremacy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no idea what he's talking about. Bringing up the independent state of Croatia? I mean, this was in the Second World War, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't this repeated in the beginning of the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We won't go into that sort of argument. Yes, you've got five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have an hour and 45 minutes after the break, because I examined him only for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, you've got longer than five minutes. You've got five minutes until the break and then I think you've got another 20 minutes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then we didn't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say yourself on page 4, in paragraph 4 that you went to see the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Jerko Doko?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he told you then what you were supposed to do with the records of military conscripts and how you should obstruct the army.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't Jerko who received me. He wasn't at work then. But I was received by Munib Bisic, his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right Munib Bisic, a Muslim, and Jerko Doko is a Croat; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: These are legal representatives of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Legal representatives. And you're a legal representative too, and you as a Muslim are the legal representative that obstructed his very own function, and he concealed the military records that was in his hands on the basis of his official duty.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I hid it from the Yugoslav army who wanted to take it out of my province of work, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the Yugoslav army want to do with these documents?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: What was I supposed to do if they took these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you care about that? You're not the superior of the Yugoslav People's Army. As secretary for the Secretariat for National Defence in a municipality like Bratunac, you're not their superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must slow this down. You must both remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that you were advised when you went to the ministry that you should keep the records in a secret place?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was told that these records should not fall into the hands of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And why didn't you give the Serbs the documents that pertained to the Serbs only when they asked you for it?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Because physically this documentation could not be split up, because it was filed in alphabetical order and they came with the Yugoslav army on that day to take it away and they asked for this to be done immediately and it could not have been done immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But isn't it true that they only asked you for their parts of the files, the records?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: On that day, they asked so that the Yugoslav People's Army would not go back without having done anything. They said, "Give us at least the documents pertaining to Serbs." But physically it could not have been done that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that all the incidents on the 27th of August, 1991 would have been overcome only if you had given the Serbs their very own records, the records they asked for? Also, it doesn't have to do with lists only. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't answer that, as to what would have happened. He's answered that you couldn't split them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these records were not compiled according to certain lists, the way you are trying to portray it now, or rather, every military conscript has a file of his own?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Every conscript has a file of his own, but the files are in alphabetical order, so one could not know who is a Serb and who is a Muslim. And in this big file that weighed about 30 kilogrammes, there were about 50 or 100 military files respectively, so one file had to be looked at at a time, so this required at least seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many military conscripts were there in the municipality of Bratunac, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: All military conscripts, all who would serve their military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there? How many did you have in your records in the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't count, but all the Muslims and Serbs were on this list of the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not bringing that into question at all, that there were Muslims and Serbs on this list. I'm asking you about the files, the records. How many files, records, did you have in total? This is an elementary figure which you should be aware of.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do any counting. And believe me, I do not know this particular figure, what the overall number was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that, that you are not aware of that. But let's proceed. On page 6, paragraph 2, you say that the Serbs from Kravica and Bratunac, after the killing of two Muslims, evacuated women and children to Ljubovija because they were afraid that the Muslims would seek revenge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: This was staged, this moving out, because nobody was threatened by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This will be a sensible moment to stop. We're moving on to another topic. We'll adjourn, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you were told you could have two hours. You've had one hour, 40 minutes. You can have another 25 minutes, an extra five.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there's no possibility of extending that time, is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I'll try and make it brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becirevic, would you please give me short answers, yourself. You say that you launched an attack on Kravica and that you did so because you were hungry. That's what you say on page 3, paragraph 4, of your statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: For me to give -- be able to give you yes or no answers, I have to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. actually explain a bit, expound. But as you just want to hear yes or no, I'm not going to be able to say either, give you a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, why -- did you attack Kravica and why did you do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 17th of April, 1992 -- or rather, from that date up until the 7th of January, we were under a complete siege, and it was precisely because of that complete siege we had no possibility of having any assistance in the way of food, clothing, or anything else brought in to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on that occasion - and I'm quoting you - you say, "We decided to set up a corridor for the women and children wishing to leave the village. Once we'd entered the village, we just came across soldiers who had decided to stay on and fight." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: What date did you launch your attack on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The beginning of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did that on the 7th of January, 1993; isn't that so, Mr. Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the 7th of January is precisely Orthodox Christmas, so you attacked the place for the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's how it turned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That's how it turned out, did it? Now, is it also true that in addition to Kravica, on that same day you attacked the other hamlets, Brana, Bacici [phoen], Popovici, Mandici [phoen] and so on, Popravdici, which make up an area of about 2.300 inhabitants together with Kravica, which is where the older Serb school is located, which was erected in 1864; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you attacked the Serbs on their Christmas. You say you left a corridor open for women and children and that it was just the soldiers who remained. Now, do you know, for instance, that you slaughtered Mara Bozic, born in 1909, a lady who was born in 1909, her throat was cut; Kristina Eric, another elderly woman; Risto Popovic, born in 1920, a man; Vaso Nikolic, born in 1920; Mitar Nikolic, 1927. Those are their dates of birth. Ljubica Obacki, another woman, born in 1918; Vladimir Stojanovic, born in 1915; and so on and so forth. You killed them, you slit their throats, you slit the throats of elderly men and women, and only three soldiers were killed, only three military-able men, in fact, not to say soldiers. Men of fighting age. Is that right, or not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the names. I can't tell you. You can read out any number of names you like, I don't know the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know who the people were whose throats were slit in Kravica, that they were all elderly people, men and women?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that that was what happened at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that in the attack, in addition to you, there was Naser Oric taking part, Zulfo Tursunovic, Ferid Hodzic, Becir Mehanic [phoen], Bajra Osmanovic nicknamed Mis [phoen] or mouse, Nedjad Bektic [phoen], Hadija Mehulic [phoen], Veiz Sabic, Nedjad Set [phoen], and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just reading out a list of names makes it quite impossible for the witness to answer. But more seriously, what is alleged is that -- Wait a moment. He can deal with the allegation you make. What is suggested is that, during the attack, the throats of old people were cut. Now, is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's no truth in that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are facts and figures about all these persons killed, Mr. Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there for me to be able to have seen that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't participate in the attack on Kravica.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in the attack on Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, then, please: On that same day, in addition to Kravica, did you also attack the village of Siljkovici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That belonged to the area of the Kravica local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all that belongs to Konjevic Polje, does it not, that general area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: But from that place called Kravica, for a full eight months, on a daily basis dozens of women and children were killed in Konjevic Polje. So Kravica is the place from which most of the grenades, shell -- tank shells, Howitzer attacks and so on were launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to those tanks and Howitzers, you stormed the place and slaughtered these elderly people, and Siljkovici was another place you attacked on Christmas Day; isn't that right? Is it right or not?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That was a military operation of the classical type, in a counter onslaught, a counterattack on the forces of the Bosnian Serbs, and quite normally this was done in military fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you consider that to be military fashion, do you? All right. On the 16th of January, did you attack the village of Cosici, where you also slaughtered 15 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of that village at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, did you attack the village of Kusici and killed a further 20 Serbs there too?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Those villages are around the Srebrenica area. I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you attack Skelani and kill 13 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Once again, the Srebrenica municipality, which I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't take part in that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was only in Konjevic Polje and defended Konjevic Polje. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, tell me this, please: I'm asking you about the rest of the villages in the Bratunac area. Did you take part on the Bljeceva attack on the 6th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It's got nothing to do with the free territories of Konjevic Polje. That is a local community which gravitated towards Srebrenica. So the forces from Konjevic Polje were not able to do anything of the sort because of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about how Kosana Zekic, an old lady in the village of Bijena [phoen] was slaughtered on the 6th of May along with three other Serbs. Radojko Milosevic was burnt alive.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, those villages are not around Konjevic Polje, so don't ask me about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the 6th of May is once again a religious holiday? It is St. George's Day, Djurdjevdan.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Let me state again they are all villages around Srebrenica and I have nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the attack on the village of Oparci on the 1st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Never heard of the village of Oparci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the attack on the village of Metaljka on the 2nd of June 1992? Did you take part in that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's Cers Gordi [phoen], Vlasenica municipality. Once again, we have nothing to do with that. No forces from Konjevic Polje at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Ferid Hodzic from Cerska? Do you know about him? He completely destroyed the village.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I did see Ferid Hodzic during the siege of Konjevic Polje in Cerska, so I know the man. I can say I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the attack on the Rupovo Brdo village on the 10th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Once again, the Vlasenica municipality, with which I or the units from Konjevic Polje had nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who did they have something to do with, the units from Konjevic Polje? Only with the village of Kravica, nobody else?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you want an exact answer, they had things to do with the Milici unit, which is the Semiser [phoen] region, and in that region no Serb village was burnt to the ground. There was the Drina River there on the opposite side, so that the people they did have contact with was Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your responsibility only stretched to Kravica, to include Kravica; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: If you were to look at the Konjevic Polje units and the Kravica and so on, I see no responsibility there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the old lady and the old men you slaughtered? That's no -- you have no military accountability and responsibility for that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The units from Konjevic Polje never perpetrated those acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you take part in the attack on the village of Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Once again, you're mentioning a village around Srebrenica with which I have nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
