utterances.text: You're wasting your time and ours going over these matters which are outside the witness's knowledge. If it's relevant, you will be allowed to call evidence about these matters. But it's no good trying to attack the witness with matters which he knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, in view of the post he held and the region concerned, it is my assumption that he did know about it. The fact that he says he doesn't know about it is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard what he says and you're -- you are bound by his answer. He doesn't know about it. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am moving on, Mr. May, and I will prove that he had every knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the attack on the Serbian village of Loznica on the 28th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Once again you're asking a question about something that the units in Konjevic Polje had nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the village of Brezane? Anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know how far that is from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the village of Zagone?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Once again, the same answer; nothing to do with that. Konjevic Polje has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you take part in the attack on the Serbian village of Krnjici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's far away somewhere again. So my answer is the same as to your other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the attacks on these villages. You and your colleagues in the headquarters, the staff, you didn't dovetail your actions and have anything to do with those villages?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Accused, you must understand that Konjevic Polje was a separate enclave, quite separate from the Srebrenica enclave, and it really did have nothing to do, have any contacts with them in the course of 1992, right until these areas fell, and the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the village of Zalazje, an attack there when 39 Serbs were killed and slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: My answer is the same. Konjevic Polje is a long way away, 30 kilometres away and has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about the attack on Laducic [phoen]? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Kravica separated the enclave of Konjevic Polje from the free territories around Srebrenica, so that any attempt to pass through that terrain was sanctioned, that is to say, there were ambushes set up by the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the attack on the Erzestica village on the 2nd of August when 55 houses were set alight and Serbs killed there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Once again, this came under the responsibility of the Srebrenica units and we from Konjevic Polje had nothing to do physically with the village of Erzestica and the people who were there will be able to bear this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you read out all the remaining attacks which you allege and the witness can deal with that, rather than this time-wasting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that you had some military operations underway in Milici; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said we just had a defence line up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You call it a defence line. On the 24th of September, did you in fact, in the Serbian village Podravinja, kill 31 Serbs from the village?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The accused is once again saying the same thing. As you're not from the area, I can't answer that question. Konjevic Polje did not have a defence line towards Podravinja because, once again, that is some 30 to 40 kilometres away and is in between the forces of the Bosnian Serbs and the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Becirevic. Could you then tell me at least how many Serbs were killed at your hand and by your hand?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Thank God by my hand not a single Serb was killed. Now, how many Bosniaks fell victim to the Serbs, and in Bratunac in the space of one month the figure was 1.000 women, children, and elderly persons without setting up any resistance, and that would have happened in Konjevic Polje had there not been resistance on the 29th of May, 1992 when the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, together with the paramilitary formations and local Serbs, suffered their first defeat in the Bratunac municipality. Up until then, the Serb forces came upon no resistance whatsoever and were able to perform ethnic cleansing, expel the population from those areas, and killed, as I said, 1.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about your own responsibility and accountability and, according to my information, you are responsible for the killing of 68 civilians in Kravica on Christmas Day 1993 and 20 civilians in Donji Magasici and Bozici. Is that true or is it not, Mr. Becirevic? You didn't question or challenge Kravica. Now I'm asking you whether you're responsible for the killing of 68 civilians in Kravica on Christmas Day 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in that at all. That is not true, and I can prove where I was on that particular day. So that's got nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And are you responsible for the killing of these detainees, amongst them Milutin Milosevic, the chief of MUP? Are you responsible for that particular killing?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what killing you're talking about. Milutin Milosevic led a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army and paramilitary formations in the attack on Konjevic Polje on the 29th of May, and in the fighting Milutin Milosevic lost his life. He was killed at Konjevic Polje. So nobody went to Bratunac at all to attack Bratunac. It was Milutin Milosevic who came with his units, with the units of the JNA, to cleanse Konjevic Polje of the people and to kill the people there. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tell me this, please: As you say that he was killed in the fighting, killed in battle, isn't it true that your fighters captured Milutin Milosevic alive, that they tortured him, killed him, and left him there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Believe me when I say that I was told that Milutin was killed in battle and that he had a loudspeaker with him at the time and that he spoke over the loudspeaker. He said, "You should kill and set fire to everything and not well-to-do houses because they're full of booty." That's what Milutin said and Milutin Berisic [phoen]. They had a loudspeaker in their hands and that's how they led the attack from the Kravica direction towards Konjevic Polje on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, that in the report by Masovjetski -- that's his famous report where he says that he was in fact killed by the Serbs so as to blame the Muslims, be able to blame the Muslims for that killing. Now, who's lying? We'll leave it up to others to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've stopped you. The witness can't answer about that report, and he's dealt with the death of this man. He's given his evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Becirevic. In paragraph 4, page 7, you speak about an event where allegedly the JNA came to Konjevic Polje in order to disarm your Muslim forces; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Just let me find it. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 7, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't find it, actually, but I know what you're talking about. I know that the Yugoslav People's Army on the 27th of April in the morning came into Konjevic Polje, encircled it, and demanded a handover of all weapons. On that day I saw with my own eyes Miroslav Deronjic dressed in uniform, who had come into my village, Hrncici, asking that Muslims turn Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. over their weapons to Serbs and saying that nothing would happen to them in return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about something in your statement, and you are now mentioning a person who was not a JNA member. He was a member of the Bratunac TO. In the same paragraph where you say that allegedly the JNA came to Konjevic Polje to disarm your Muslim forces, you say that you were not putting up resistance because there were only a few of you men with arms.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: We were not putting up resistance because we had nothing to put up resistance with, whereas they came with APCs and we couldn't resist such force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Becirevic. You say in the same paragraph, "The Serbs who had come on armoured personnel carriers, trucks with a huge amount of weapons, thus broke through our defences." That's what you say. "They tried to encircle the village and during that operation two of our men were killed and two were wounded. Since dark was falling, they decided to retreat." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Then explain, since you say you were not putting up resistance and that only a few of you had weapons, while saying at the same time that unbelievably strong Serb forces managed to break through your defences, how is that possible? How come they broke through your defences when they didn't even manage to encircle the village? At the same time, you were not putting up resistance and you had two men killed and 1992 men wounded.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to fighters who withdrew from the village when these forces came, and there was no resistance from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say they broke through your defences.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: There were no defences. They came into those villages without encountering any resistance. Nobody fired a single round. Their only intention was to seize the weapons peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You say they did not manage to encircle the village. How come they didn't manage, if you were not putting up any resistance?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: They came into every village and hamlet on APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But aren't you saying that those strong Serb forces drove away their wounded on APCs?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Not Serb wounded. What is curious is they collected those wounded Bosniaks who had been wounded by Serb forces and they drove them to Bratunac and Ljubovija for treatment. They drove them away. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your time is almost up, you should be warned. You've got two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How can you claim all this about these monstrously strong Serb forces? How can you say all that you've just said and assert that in this all-out attack on Konjevic Polje you had 11 casualties, whereas these monstrous Serb forces, monstrously strong forces, had 44 wounded?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about the 29th of May, when we put up resistance to those strong Serb forces for the first time. First of all, it was the JNA who aggressed Konjevic Polje, together with people from -- veterans from Vukovar and local forces. We put up resistance because we had seen what happened in Hranca, Glogova, in a school in a neighbouring village where 500 civilians were killed. That's why we started to put up resistance. They didn't allow these forces to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning the reasons why you fought there. You are representing the Muslim side as unarmed civilians with only a couple of men under arms, and the result, which you don't deny, is that those forces had 44 casualties, that is, four times more men killed than you did. How come those unarmed people succeeded in killing 44 soldiers of those Serb forces which were allegedly attacking you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is really the truth: We were attacked by five tank, five APCs. There was more support from artillery from Serb positions. Many barrels were trained on Konjevic Polje, which was defended exclusively by people armed with light infantry weapons. On that morning we were lucky enough to capture one APC, which had been on a reconnaissance mission, and we trained the barrel of this APC towards the attackers. That was the success we had scored. I think that was the first defeat suffered by the JNA in Bratunac municipality. And it was inflicted on them by these defenders who did not allow themselves to share the fate of other surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the problem, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had plenty of time and you've wasted much of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, during your examination-in-chief you mentioned the Red Berets today, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I mentioned them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You then mentioned convoys coming from Srebrenica towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the aviation coming from the direction of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned about a thousand or more civilians killed.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, over a month, in Bratunac and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned 12 to 15 thousand people killed in a column of moving people.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you failed to mention all that when you gave your statement on the 24th of January, 1994 and more recently this year. Why didn't you mention that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The last time I was here I spoke about everything in detail. These are the facts that I presented the last time I spoke to the investigators here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While Mr. Groome was questioning, I didn't make any objections, but all these things are not contained in the statement. If something is introduced under Rule 92 bis, I don't think we should go beyond that Rule. Otherwise, the cross-examination is prejudiced. That would be my objection as amicus curiae. I believe that the examination-in-chief should stay within the scope of the statement provided to you and to the opposing party and not go beyond it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Part of this evidence was introduced by way of 92 bis, but the other part was given live.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reason is that there may be something which the witness doesn't mention in his statement which may be important which he mentions when he comes here. Experience shows that this does happen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree with you completely. But it does prejudice my preparation for cross-examination to a certain extent. However, I appreciate your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Still, Witness, is it true that on the 1st of September, 1991 the anniversary of the establishment of Bratunac village was celebrated?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But was there a celebration of the anniversary?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't participate in that. I claim that under full responsibility. I doubt it very much that anybody could celebrate anything, because we had serious problems in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that in Bratunac a gathering of 10.000 people was addressed by Nurif?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I heard that Nurif made a speech at that rally, but I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he finished with these words: "Allah Imanet and see you on the battlefield next year"? Did you hear him say that before 10.000 people?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: He is a former JNA officer. He probably had information to that effect, and that's why he made the statement. I can't make any further comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding your statement - paragraph 4, Your Honours - you said in the first sentence: "Before the war, in the municipality there were no JNA barracks. We only had the weapons which belonged to the Territorial Defence." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: It's true that in Bratunac there were no barracks whatsoever and the only weapons were those belonging to the TO, which the JNA later removed from those depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You then go on to say, "That included mortars, recoilless guns," and you also mentioned here "rocket launchers, automatic rifles, and a lot of explosives such as grenades and mines." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That was what the report said. I never entered those depots, but from the reports, these weapons were enough to arm a brigade. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this first: These TO units throughout Yugoslavia, you as an educated man, a lawyer, do you know when this practice started wherein every municipality and every village received weapons of this sort?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I know that these weapons belonged to the people of Bratunac municipality, and it was the people of Bratunac municipality contributed funds for the purchase of these weapons. However, the Yugoslav People's Army collected the weapons and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One thing remains unclear: You've said it happened in 1989.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I said that, to the best of my recollection. It was a long time before the democratic elections held in 1990, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But here on page 2, paragraph 8, you talk about the elections and the establishment of the Municipal Assembly; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And Sabit Mujkic was commander of the Territorial Defence, and you say here that you demanded that certain decisions be made on the replacement of general managers. If this was indeed removed in 1989, did you raise this issue before the Assembly, the issue of the Territorial Defence lacking any weapons whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: When I took over that job, that post, those weapons were not there. Even if I had raised the issue, I knew it would not be returned by the JNA, so it made no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please pay attention to paragraph 27. When this column of the JNA arrived, you didn't know how to cope with it. You didn't know what to do at first.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what weapons I'm talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, did you indeed say that you didn't know what to do at first?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then somebody remembered that in the neighbouring commune there was a hand-held rocket launcher. Is that the same sort of hand-held rocket launcher that everybody in the TO had?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a Zolja hand-held rocket launcher located in Cerska. On the 29th of May, 1992 we had nothing to stop these tanks with and they broke into Konjevic Polje. It was our good fortune that they torched -- that we torched a truck that was in the middle of the road and blocked their passage, and then somebody remembered that in the neighbouring populated area there was this Zolja rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to finish quickly. So somebody remembered that in the neighbouring commune you had this weapon, and you used it to destroy the first tank, not the APC.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We used the rocket launcher, whereas the APC was transferred to the hill to fight the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing: When you removed the records of conscripts from the administration, did you also collect the entire weaponry of the Territorial Defence along with the records?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. All that was left in the Secretariat for National Defence when I came there were these papers, the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this attack that we're talking about now, would it be fair to say that by the 29th of May your village was completely surrounded by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, our village was encircled from all sides until the 29th of May. All the villages in Bratunac municipality were ethnically cleansed. Konjevic Polje was the only one still standing, and that's why they attacked it, to finish us off, to finish what they had already done in all the other local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The accused put to you correctly that Mr. Deronjic was not officially a member of the JNA. My question to you is: On the initial attack on your village, did you see Mr. Deronjic in the company of JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Deronjic was accompanying the JNA on the 27th of April when they took over the weapons and barged into our village. Deronjic was also present on the 29th of May, carrying a loudspeaker, as well as Milutin Milosevic. They were accompanying the JNA together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is: When you saw Mr. Deronjic in the company of the JNA, where precisely was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAIL BECIREVIC
utterances.text: The first time they entered, on the 27th of April, Deronjic was on top of an APC when --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness, Your Honour. I do have some information with respect to Judge Kwon's query and with respect to Defence Exhibit 134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us allow the witness to go. Mr. Becirevic, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Prosecution Exhibit 443, tab 8, as Judge Kwon pointed out, part of that exhibit were two letters that appear in some ways to be identical but yet there seem to be some differences, namely the stamp and the handwriting seems to be different. I just -- I do have some information regarding the providence of them, and we will be filing an exhibit, as I referenced, I believe, two weeks ago with respect to where these documents came from. Both of these documents came from the same place at the same time. They were received from the Republika Srpska National Assembly building, the archive, and they were tendered to us by Ms. Rajka Stanisic, the administrator of the Assembly and the person responsible for that archive. That was done with the consent of the RS government, and they were turned over to us on the 2nd of February, 1998. As Your Honours will notice, the evidence record numbers of the two documents are consecutive, indicating that they were taken into possession at the same time. Members of our staff have some ideas why there are two originally executed copies, but rather than speculate on that, if the Court thinks it is an issue, we can seek to have a statement from Mrs. Stanisic, the keeper of these records, as to how there are two copies. I would point out to Your Honours that similar documents in -- in double copies exist for the municipalities of Zvornik and a few -- and at least one other municipality, the name escapes me at the moment. But it seems to have been not irregular that two copies exist. One matter that I would point out: That Mrs. Stanisic was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. responsible for not only the Assembly archive but also the archive of the Presidency, and that may be one possible explanation as to why two copies exist. Now, with respect to D134, that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in November of 2002 in cooperation -- In cooperation with the Republika Srpska government, members of our staff were allowed to look at documents in the records of the Republika Srpska intelligence security service, and that document was found in that collection. The author of the document or anything else about the origination of the document, I'm unable to provide at this time. Your Honour, just in terms of taking stock, the Prosecution did not play an intercept, tab 1 of 443. Tab 3, we ask that it be simply marked for identification. And remainder of the exhibits, 2 and 4 through 10, the Prosecution is formally tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 1 is withdrawn. The remainder, of course, are admitted, one marked for identification. Now, Mr. Groome, the next witness is Mr. Banjanovic. We will sit until 2.00. Normally one wouldn't want to start another witness. I don't know if it's a matter for you. We will admit his statement under Rule 92 bis. Of course, we're not sitting for the next week. Do you want to make a start or leave it until next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it's all right with the Court, we would wish to make a start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, since you're under the pressure of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps while we're waiting, could I ask that exhibit numbers be assigned to both the 92 bis package and a binder of nine exhibits that we will use with this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'm not sure if we've got the exhibits. Yes, can we give them the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Rule 92 bis statement is Prosecutor's Exhibit 444, and the exhibits tab 1 to 9 will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 445.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to state your name.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Fadil Banjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber has accepted your verified statement, the statement you verified in front of a registrar last week -- or this week, I'm sorry, as Prosecution Exhibit 444, so I will be dealing with just particular aspects of your testimony. I would ask that we begin your testimony by having you look at Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 1, and ask you, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that a summary of your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Banjanovic, the Chamber has heard from other witnesses from the Zvornik municipality about some of the events leading up to the outbreak of hostilities there. I want to draw your attention to the middle of April, and I'd ask you to focus on the situation in your municipality, and would you be -- in your village. I'd ask you to begin by telling us what was the name of the village that you lived in at that time.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kozluk, the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was Kozluk with respect to the downtown area of Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kozluk is on the Drina River in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the road leading from Zvornik to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And approximately how many kilometres outside of Zvornik is it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you also help orient the Chamber. Approximately how -- are you familiar with the village of Celopek? And if so, where is that with respect to Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Celopek is one of the Serb villages in the municipality of Zvornik, and it is on the road from Zvornik to Bijeljina, towards Kozluk. That's where Celopek is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can return to my initial question to you: At the time that hostilities broke out in the Zvornik municipality by the middle of April, can you please characterise your situation in your commune of Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Kozluk was a multi-ethnic community, and it was quite peaceful. While, for example, in the surrounding villages, there were quite a few clashes and hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was your position within the commune of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to the beginning of the 5th of April, did you make a written announcement to the citizens of Kozluk, encouraging them to remain peaceful and to try to avoid confrontation?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 2. I'm handing the original to you. A copy of this will be visible on the screens in the courtroom. Is that the announcement that you made?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you just to read paragraphs 4 and then paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: "We call on the local population not to further undermine trust already significantly undermined and to preserve co-existence and a life together."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if you would, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: "We call upon all citizens to gather tomorrow at 1800 hours for a rally, a peace rally that will be held at the centre of Kozluk, which will be attended also by the citizens of the local communes of Tabanci, Malesic, Rijic, and Skocic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did such a peace rally take place?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once again, to avoid confrontation, did the -- did citizens of Kozluk surrender their weapons upon the demand of local Serb authorities of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 3. I'm handing -- having the original handed to you. Can you please describe for us what is this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: This involves the citizens of Kozluk, both Bosniaks and Serbs. 90 per cent of them are hunters who had their own hunting guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without going through the specific weapons that are detailed on that document, can you just generally characterise the type of weapons that were turned over and memorialised on that receipt.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We handed the weapons over through a commission that consisted of a few citizens of Kozluk. The weapons were registered. They were German-made, and also there were a few pistols that were privately owned and duly registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you some questions about whether or not an attack occurred on Kozluk. My question to you for this -- at this stage is simply: Was there an attack on Kozluk, and can you give us the date that that attack began?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was shooting often around Kozluk, and large-scale national tensions were on the rise. Big military and paramilitary units passed through there and the situation was tense, generally speaking. During the night between the 20th and 21st, a staged attack took place against Kozluk, carried out by various formations from the surrounding places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I will ask you some detailed questions about that. But what I'm interested in now is the period of time between April and the 20th of June. During that time period, was there any outright violence in the village of Kozluk during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe it or characterise it to the extent of that violence?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was pressure against the citizens themselves who were trying to live peacefully. These pressures had to do with the increasingly frequent shooting that took place. Grenades were thrown. There was intimidation. Military, paramilitary, and other units went on with incursions into Kozluk itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Towards the latter part of May, the Yugoslav People's Army formally withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you in a position in Kozluk to see any of those troops as they withdrew from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, we were totally surrounded. Long columns of military vehicles went through Kozluk. They involved tanks, APCs, trucks with JNA insignia, with a five-pointed star and the flag. What we found strange was that this was no longer the Yugoslav People's Army, the one where I did my military service. In these vehicles and on these vehicles one could see men with fur hats, cockades, wearing beards, who were shouting, throwing bottles in the centre of Kozluk, stopping vehicles, and also satisfying their physiological needs on the road itself. This was not the Yugoslav People's Army where I had done my military service and where other people had done their military service. Many columns were moving along the road between Zvornik and Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, during this period of time, after the beginning of April and up until the 20th of June, could members of the Kozluk community, could they travel down to the town of Zvornik? Would they be permitted to do so?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were they permitted to travel to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any place that people in Kozluk could go if they wanted -- if they chose to leave Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was Loznica, and other places in Serbia, with special passes issued by the authorities in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How was that communicated to the people of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, we were surrounded. Serb guards and barricades from neighbouring villages were all around us. The Serb police that was in Kozluk could issue passes for those citizens who wished to go to Serbia. However, major financial resources were required for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did some people from Kozluk in fact leave Kozluk and go to Serbia or through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the situation surrounding Kozluk became significantly, or so dangerous that you yourself wished to leave Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were there other people in Kozluk who had a similar desire?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those people who remained in Kozluk were subjected to all-out pressure. Most people wanted to leave Kozluk peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it your intention to permanently leave Kozluk or leave until the security situation stabilised and it was safe to return?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: We wanted to leave temporarily because we were totally surrounded, unarmed. We had surrendered our weapons and our life was in danger. Some people had already been killed in Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've described the village as coming under attack between the 20th and the 21st of June. I'd ask you to describe the situation in Kozluk between the 20th and the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was disastrous. One could no longer speak of co-existence, tolerance, because long columns of vehicles were passing through the village. There was shooting coming from all sides. The frontline was nearby, so paramilitary formations often came to Kozluk wanting to take away younger persons and to commit other crimes. The situation was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to the morning of the 26th of June. On that morning, were there vehicles -- military vehicles positioned in the area of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I got up in the morning, I saw a large concentration of people in the centre of Kozluk, and I saw a large number of military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what types of military vehicles you saw.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the centre of Kozluk itself, three tanks were deployed. There were several military personnel carriers, trucks, and all of this was in the centre of Kozluk, near the culture centre, and the barrels were aimed at houses where people lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know two men by the name of Branko Grujic and Jovo Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Brano Grujic was the mayor of the municipality of Zvornik and he was supposed to be the mayor of all citizens, Brano Grujic was. Jovo Mijatovic was our member of parliament. He was elected by all of us and he was in the higher authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, is he also called Branko, rather than Brano?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know him as Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you summoned to a meeting with these two men on the 26th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A Serb policeman came to pick me up, and he took me to the police station in Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise for us what was said to you at the meeting with these two men.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the police station in Kozluk, in the police there were several local policemen, there were a few men in uniform, in military uniform, and I saw the mayor, Brano Grujic, and Mijatovic, the MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to focus for the moment on what exactly did they say to you during the course of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a meeting. Quite simply, Brano Grujic said to me that "Within 60 minutes I have to gather together all the people and that we have to leave Kozluk urgently." I asked him, "Go where?" And he said that we would be going towards Serbia. I asked him -- I mean, we had no vehicles, we had no fuel, and he said to me that everything was ready and that within one hour's time everything would be in the centre of Kozluk; the buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've said that he said "everyone." Did he literally mean every person living in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: This order applied exclusively to the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he mean literally every Bosniak living in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just -- we are a bit past time. When you get to a convenient moment, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one more question, Your Honour, I think would be a good place to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe what was going on in Kozluk at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time that you were meeting with them. When you returned to where you lived in Kozluk, can you describe what was happening in the village.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC
utterances.text: Next to every house there were two or three military personnel standing there. Kozluk has more than 1.000 houses, so there were more than 1.000 soldiers, or rather, military persons, belonging to the police or soldiers in military uniforms, and a large number of people generally wearing different types of uniforms, with masks on their heads, gloves on, and these were in fact paramilitary units. And they pushed the people back like sheep towards the centre of Kozluk. They shot, they set fire to certain houses and facilities, and in the process they wounded several of the local people. I realised that this was no peaceful exit. We were becoming hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll continue my examination a week from Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, we have to adjourn now because it is the time when we do adjourn. We are not sitting next week as a court, the reason being that we have allowed the accused more preparation time next week. That's the reason that we are not sitting. I'm sorry that your evidence has been broken up and you will have to come back. But would you be back, please, on Monday week to continue your evidence. During this adjournment and any others there may be, don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over and don't let anybody speak to you about it. That includes members of the Prosecution team. Although, you can, of course, speak to them about your travel arrangements and the like. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 2.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 19th day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
